Now, say, Chatillon, what would France with us?
Now then, Chatillon, tell us: what does the King of France want with us?
Thus, after greeting, speaks the King of France, / In my behaviour, to the majesty, / The borrow'd majesty of England here.
After his greetings, the King of France speaks like this, through me, to the majesty of England: the borrowed majesty of England.
A strange way to begin: "borrowed majesty"!
Silence, good mother; hear the embassy.
Quiet, mother. Hear the message out.

Philip of France, in right and true behalf / Of thy deceased brother Geffrey's son, / Arthur Plantagenet, lays most lawful claim / To this fair island and the territories,— / To Ireland, Poictiers, Anjou, Touraine, Maine; / Desiring thee to lay aside the sword / Which sways usurpingly these several titles, / And put the same into young Arthur's hand, / Thy nephew and right royal sovereign.

Philip of France, acting rightly on behalf of your dead brother Geoffrey's son, Arthur Plantagenet, lays fully lawful claim to this island and its territories: Ireland, Poitiers, Anjou, Touraine and Maine. He asks you to put down the sword that wrongfully rules these lands and hand them to young Arthur, your nephew and true king.
What follows if we disallow of this?
And what happens if we refuse?
The proud control of fierce and bloody war, / To enforce these rights so forcibly withheld.
The proud force of fierce and bloody war, to win back the rights you are holding by force.
Here have we war for war, and blood for blood, / Controlment for controlment;—so answer France.
Then we meet war with war, blood with blood, force with force. Give France that answer.
Then take my king's defiance from my mouth, / The farthest limit of my embassy.
Then take my king's defiance from my lips. That is as far as my message goes.

Bear mine to him, and so depart in peace: / Be thou as lightning in the eyes of France; / For ere thou canst report I will be there, / The thunder of my cannon shall be heard: / So, hence! Be thou the trumpet of our wrath, / And sullen presage of your own decay.— / An honourable conduct let him have:— / Pembroke, look to 't. Farewell, Chatillon.

Take my defiance back to him and leave in peace. Be like lightning in France's eyes, because before you can report I'll be there, and the thunder of my cannon will be heard. Go! Be the trumpet of my anger and the gloomy warning of your own ruin. (To his lords) Give him an honourable escort. Pembroke, see to it. Goodbye, Chatillon.

What now, my son! Have I not ever said / How that ambitious Constance would not cease / Till she had kindled France and all the world / Upon the right and party of her son? / This might have been prevented and made whole / With very easy arguments of love; / Which now the manage of two kingdoms must / With fearful bloody issue arbitrate.

What did I tell you, my son? Haven't I always said that ambitious Constance would never rest until she had set France and the whole world on fire for her son's claim? This could have been prevented and settled with easy, friendly talks. Now two kingdoms will have to decide it by fearful, bloody fighting.
Our strong possession and our right for us.
We have strong possession and right on our side.
Your strong possession much more than your right, / Or else it must go wrong with you and me: / So much my conscience whispers in your ear, / Which none but heaven and you and I shall hear.
Strong possession, much more than right, or things will go badly for you and me. That's what my conscience whispers in your ear, and only heaven, you and I will hear it.
My liege, here is the strangest controversy, / Come from the country to be judg'd by you, / That e'er I heard: shall I produce the men?
My lord, here is the strangest dispute I ever heard of, brought from the country for you to judge. Shall I bring in the men?
Our abbeys and our priories shall pay / This expedition's charge.
Our abbeys and priories will pay for this war.

Your faithful subject I, a gentleman / Born in Northamptonshire, and eldest son, / As I suppose, to Robert Falconbridge,— / A soldier by the honour-giving hand / Of Coeur-de-lion knighted in the field.
Your loyal subject, a gentleman born in Northamptonshire, and, I suppose, eldest son of Robert Falconbridge, a soldier knighted on the battlefield by the honour-giving hand of Richard the Lionheart.
The son and heir to that same Falconbridge.
The son and heir of that same Falconbridge.
Is that the elder, and art thou the heir? / You came not of one mother then, it seems.
He is the elder and you are the heir? You can't have had the same mother, then.

Most certain of one mother, mighty king,— / That is well known; and, as I think, one father: / But for the certain knowledge of that truth / I put you o'er to heaven and to my mother:— / Of that I doubt, as all men's children may.

We certainly had the same mother, great king; everyone knows that. And I think the same father too. But for certain knowledge of that, I refer you to heaven and to my mother. I'm as unsure of it as any man's children can be.
Out on thee, rude man! thou dost shame thy mother, / And wound her honour with this diffidence.
Shame on you, you rude man! You disgrace your mother and wound her honour with this doubt.

I, madam? no, I have no reason for it,— / That is my brother's plea, and none of mine; / The which if he can prove, 'a pops me out / At least from fair five hundred pound a-year: / Heaven guard my mother's honour and my land!

Me, madam? No, I have no reason to doubt it. That's my brother's case, not mine. If he can prove it, he knocks me out of at least five hundred pounds a year. Heaven protect my mother's honour, and my land!
A good blunt fellow.—Why, being younger born, / Doth he lay claim to thine inheritance?
A good plain-spoken fellow. (To Robert) Why do you, the younger son, claim his inheritance?

I know not why, except to get the land. / But once he slander'd me with bastardy: / But whe'er I be as true begot or no, / That still I lay upon my mother's head; / But that I am as well begot, my liege,— / Fair fall the bones that took the pains for me!— / Compare our faces and be judge yourself. / If old Sir Robert did beget us both, / And were our father, and this son like him,— / O old Sir Robert, father, on my knee / I give heaven thanks I was not like to thee!

I don't know why, unless it's to get the land. He once called me a bastard. Whether or not I was conceived honestly, that's for my mother to answer. But look how well made I am, my lord (bless the bones that took the trouble to make me!): compare our faces and judge for yourself. If old Sir Robert fathered us both and this son looks like him, then, old Sir Robert, father, I kneel and thank heaven I don't look like you!
Why, what a madcap hath heaven lent us here!
What a wild fellow heaven has sent us here!
He hath a trick of Coeur-de-lion's face; / The accent of his tongue affecteth him: / Do you not read some tokens of my son / In the large composition of this man?
He has a look of the Lionheart's face, and his voice sounds like him. Don't you see signs of my son Richard in this man's big build?
Mine eye hath well examined his parts, / And finds them perfect Richard.—Sirrah, speak, / What doth move you to claim your brother's land?
I've looked him over carefully, and he is Richard exactly. (To Robert) You, speak: why do you claim your brother's land?
Because he hath a half-face, like my father; / With half that face would he have all my land: / A half-fac'd groat five hundred pound a-year!
Because he has a thin half-face, like my father. With half a face he wants all my land: a thin-faced little coin worth five hundred pounds a year!
My gracious liege, when that my father liv'd, / Your brother did employ my father much,—
My gracious lord, when my father was alive, your brother Richard made great use of him...
Well, sir, by this you cannot get my land: / Your tale must be how he employ'd my mother.
Well, sir, that won't get you my land. Your story should be about how he made use of my mother.

And once despatch'd him in an embassy / To Germany, there with the emperor / To treat of high affairs touching that time. / The advantage of his absence took the King, / And in the meantime sojourn'd at my father's; / Where how he did prevail I shame to speak,— / But truth is truth: large lengths of seas and shores / Between my father and my mother lay,— / As I have heard my father speak himself,— / When this same lusty gentleman was got. / Upon his death-bed he by will bequeath'd / His lands to me; and took it, on his death, / That this, my mother's son, was none of his; / And if he were, he came into the world / Full fourteen weeks before the course of time. / Then, good my liege, let me have what is mine, / My father's land, as was my father's will.

And once he sent him on an embassy to the Emperor in Germany, to discuss important business of the time. The King took advantage of his absence and stayed at my father's house in the meantime. How he succeeded there I'm ashamed to say, but truth is truth: great stretches of sea and land lay between my father and my mother, as I've heard my father say himself, when this lusty gentleman was conceived. On his deathbed he left his lands to me in his will, and swore as he died that this son of my mother's was not his, and if he was, he was born a full fourteen weeks early. So, my good lord, let me have what's mine, my father's land, as my father willed.

Sirrah, your brother is legitimate; / Your father's wife did after wedlock bear him; / And if she did play false, the fault was hers; / Which fault lies on the hazards of all husbands / That marry wives. Tell me, how if my brother, / Who, as you say, took pains to get this son, / Had of your father claim'd this son for his? / In sooth, good friend, your father might have kept / This calf, bred from his cow, from all the world; / In sooth, he might; then, if he were my brother's, / My brother might not claim him; nor your father, / Being none of his, refuse him. This concludes,— / My mother's son did get your father's heir; / Your father's heir must have your father's land.

Sir, your brother is legitimate. Your father's wife gave birth to him in wedlock, and if she was unfaithful, that's her fault, a risk every husband takes when he marries. Tell me: suppose my brother, who you say fathered this son, had claimed him from your father as his own? Honestly, friend, your father could have kept this calf, born from his cow, against the whole world. He could. So even if he was my brother's, my brother couldn't claim him, and your father, though the boy wasn't his, couldn't refuse him. So this is the verdict: my mother's son fathered your father's heir, and your father's heir must have your father's land.
Shall then my father's will be of no force / To dispossess that child which is not his?
So my father's will has no power to disinherit a child who isn't his?
Of no more force to dispossess me, sir, / Than was his will to get me, as I think.
No more power to disinherit me, sir, than his will had to father me, I think.
Whether hadst thou rather be a Falconbridge, / And like thy brother, to enjoy thy land, / Or the reputed son of Coeur-de-lion, / Lord of thy presence and no land beside?
Which would you rather be: a Falconbridge, like your brother, and enjoy your land, or the reputed son of the Lionheart, master of your own fine person and no land besides?

Madam, an if my brother had my shape / And I had his, Sir Robert's his, like him; / And if my legs were two such riding-rods, / My arms such eel-skins stuff'd, my face so thin / That in mine ear I durst not stick a rose / Lest men should say 'Look where three-farthings goes!' / And, to his shape, were heir to all this land, / Would I might never stir from off this place, / I would give it every foot to have this face; / I would not be Sir Nob in any case.

Madam, if my brother had my shape and I had his, Sir Robert's shape, like him; if my legs were two thin riding-sticks, my arms like stuffed eel-skins, my face so thin I didn't dare stick a rose behind my ear in case people said "Look, there goes a three-farthing coin!"; and if, with that shape, I were heir to all this land, I'd give up every foot of it to have this face. I swear I'd never be Sir Nobody for anything.
I like thee well: wilt thou forsake thy fortune, / Bequeath thy land to him, and follow me? / I am a soldier, and now bound to France.
I like you. Will you give up your fortune, leave your land to him and follow me? I'm a soldier now, bound for France.
Brother, take you my land, I'll take my chance: / Your face hath got five hundred pound a-year; / Yet sell your face for fivepence and 'tis dear.— / Madam, I'll follow you unto the death.
Brother, you take my land, I'll take my chance. Your face has earned you five hundred pounds a year, but sell your face for fivepence and it's overpriced. Madam, I'll follow you to the death.
Nay, I would have you go before me thither.
No, I'd rather you went ahead of me there.
Our country manners give our betters way.
Our country manners let our betters go first.
Philip, my liege, so is my name begun; / Philip, good old Sir Robert's wife's eldest son.
Philip, my lord, that's how my name begins: Philip, eldest son of good old Sir Robert's wife.
From henceforth bear his name whose form thou bear'st: / Kneel thou down Philip, but rise more great,— / Arise Sir Richard and Plantagenet.
From now on, bear the name of the man whose shape you bear. Kneel down Philip, but rise up greater: arise, Sir Richard Plantagenet.
Brother by the mother's side, give me your hand: / My father gave me honour, yours gave land.— / Now blessed be the hour, by night or day, / When I was got, Sir Robert was away!
Brother on my mother's side, give me your hand. My father gave me honour, yours gave you land. Blessed be the hour, night or day, when I was conceived and Sir Robert was away!
The very spirit of Plantagenet!— / I am thy grandam, Richard; call me so.
The true spirit of the Plantagenets! I am your grandmother, Richard. Call me that.

Madam, by chance, but not by truth; what though? / Something about, a little from the right, / In at the window, or else o'er the hatch; / Who dares not stir by day must walk by night; / And have is have, however men do catch: / Near or far off, well won is still well shot; / And I am I, howe'er I was begot.

By chance, madam, not by lawful descent; so what? A bit off the straight road, in through the window or over the half-door: who doesn't dare move by day must walk at night. Having is having, however you catch it. Near or far, a good hit is a good shot, and I am who I am, however I was conceived.
Go, Falconbridge; now hast thou thy desire: / A landless knight makes thee a landed squire.— / Come, madam,—and come, Richard; we must speed / For France, for France, for it is more than need.
Go, Falconbridge, you have what you wanted: a landless knight makes you a landed squire. Come, madam, and come, Richard. We must hurry to France; it's more than necessary.
Brother, adieu. Good fortune come to thee! / For thou wast got i' th' way of honesty.
Goodbye, brother. Good luck to you, since you were conceived the honest way.

A foot of honour better than I was; / But many a many foot of land the worse. / Well, now can I make any Joan a lady:— / 'Good den, Sir Richard:'—'God-a-mercy, fellow:'— / And if his name be George, I'll call him Peter: / For new-made honour doth forget men's names: / 'Tis too respective and too sociable / For your conversion. Now your traveller,— / He and his toothpick at my worship's mess;— / And when my knightly stomach is suffic'd, / Why then I suck my teeth, and catechize / My picked man of countries:—'My dear sir,'— / Thus leaning on mine elbow I begin,— / 'I shall beseech you'—that is question now; / And then comes answer like an ABC-book:— / 'O sir,' says answer 'at your best command; / At your employment; at your service, sir:'— / 'No, sir,' says question 'I, sweet sir, at yours: / And so, ere answer knows what question would,— / Saving in dialogue of compliment, / And talking of the Alps and Apennines, / The Pyrenean and the river Po,— / It draws toward supper in conclusion so. / But this is worshipful society, / And fits the mounting spirit like myself: / For he is but a bastard to the time, / That doth not smack of observation,— / And so am I, whether I smack or no; / And not alone in habit and device, / Exterior form, outward accoutrement, / But from the inward motion to deliver / Sweet, sweet, sweet poison for the age's tooth; / Which, though I will not practise to deceive, / Yet, to avoid deceit, I mean to learn; / For it shall strew the footsteps of my rising.— / But who comes in such haste in riding-robes? / What woman-post is this? hath she no husband / That will take pains to blow a horn before her?

I'm a foot higher in honour than I was, but many, many feet of land poorer. Well, now I can make any common girl a lady. "Good evening, Sir Richard." "Thank you, fellow." And if his name is George I'll call him Peter, because newly made gentlemen forget people's names; remembering them is too polite and too friendly for someone who has just changed rank. Now take your well-travelled man: he sits at my lordship's table with his toothpick, and when my knightly stomach is full I suck my teeth and question my fancy man of the world. "My dear sir," I begin, leaning on my elbow, "may I ask you..." That's the question. And then the answer comes like a child's catechism: "O sir," says the answer, "at your command, at your disposal, at your service, sir." "No, sir," says the question, "I, sweet sir, am at yours." And so, before the answer knows what the question wants, apart from swapping compliments and talking about the Alps and the Apennines, the Pyrenees and the river Po, it's nearly supper time. But this is high society, and it suits a rising spirit like me. Anyone who doesn't pick up the fashions is only a bastard of his age, and I'm a bastard whether I pick them up or not. Not just in dress and badges and outward show, but from within I mean to serve up sweet, sweet, sweet poison for the age's taste: flattery. I won't use it to deceive, but I'll learn it so as not to be deceived, because it will smooth the path of my rise. But who's this coming in such a hurry, in riding clothes? What female messenger is this? Has she no husband to blow a horn before her?
O me, 'tis my mother!—How now, good lady! / What brings you here to court so hastily?
Oh no, it's my mother! Well, good lady, what brings you to court in such a hurry?
Where is that slave, thy brother? where is he / That holds in chase mine honour up and down?
Where is that wretch, your brother? Where is the man who hunts my honour up and down?
My brother Robert? old Sir Robert's son? / Colbrand the giant, that same mighty man? / Is it Sir Robert's son that you seek so?
My brother Robert? Old Sir Robert's son? Colbrand the giant, that mighty man? Is it Sir Robert's son you're looking for?
Sir Robert's son! Ay, thou unreverend boy, / Sir Robert's son: why scorn'st thou at Sir Robert? / He is Sir Robert's son, and so art thou.
Sir Robert's son! Yes, you disrespectful boy, Sir Robert's son. Why do you mock Sir Robert? He is Sir Robert's son, and so are you.
James Gurney, wilt thou give us leave awhile?
James Gurney, would you leave us alone for a while?
Philip—sparrow!—James, / There's toys abroad:—anon I'll tell thee more.
"Philip"? I'm no pet sparrow! James, there's news going round. I'll tell you more later.

Madam, I was not old Sir Robert's son; / Sir Robert might have eat his part in me / Upon Good-Friday, and ne'er broke his fast. / Sir Robert could do well: marry, to confess, / Could not get me; Sir Robert could not do it,— / We know his handiwork:—therefore, good mother, / To whom am I beholding for these limbs? / Sir Robert never holp to make this leg.

Madam, I wasn't old Sir Robert's son. Sir Robert could have eaten his share of me on Good Friday without breaking his fast. Sir Robert did well enough, but, to be honest, he couldn't father me; Sir Robert couldn't do it. We know his handiwork. So, good mother, whom do I owe these limbs to? Sir Robert never helped make this leg.
Hast thou conspired with thy brother too, / That for thine own gain shouldst defend mine honour? / What means this scorn, thou most untoward knave?
Have you plotted with your brother too, when for your own good you should defend my honour? What do you mean by this scorn, you ill-mannered rascal?

Knight, knight, good mother,—Basilisco-like; / What! I am dubb'd; I have it on my shoulder. / But, mother, I am not Sir Robert's son: / I have disclaim'd Sir Robert and my land; / Legitimation, name, and all is gone: / Then, good my mother, let me know my father,— / Some proper man, I hope: who was it, mother?

Knight, knight, good mother, like the braggart in the old play: look, I've been dubbed, I have it on my shoulder. But mother, I'm not Sir Robert's son. I've given up Sir Robert and my land; my legitimacy, name and everything is gone. So, good mother, tell me who my father is. Some fine man, I hope. Who was it, mother?
Hast thou denied thyself a Falconbridge?
Have you denied that you are a Falconbridge?
As faithfully as I deny the devil.
As sincerely as I deny the devil.

King Richard Coeur-de-lion was thy father: / By long and vehement suit I was seduc'd / To make room for him in my husband's bed:— / Heaven lay not my transgression to my charge!— / Thou art the issue of my dear offence, / Which was so strongly urg'd, past my defence.

King Richard the Lionheart was your father. After his long, passionate wooing I was seduced into making room for him in my husband's bed. Heaven, do not hold my sin against me! You are the child of my sweet offence, which he pressed so hard I could not defend myself.

Now, by this light, were I to get again, / Madam, I would not wish a better father. / Some sins do bear their privilege on earth, / And so doth yours; your fault was not your folly: / Needs must you lay your heart at his dispose,— / Subjected tribute to commanding love,— / Against whose fury and unmatched force / The aweless lion could not wage the fight / Nor keep his princely heart from Richard's hand: / He that perforce robs lions of their hearts / May easily win a woman's. Ay, my mother, / With all my heart I thank thee for my father! / Who lives and dares but say, thou didst not well / When I was got, I'll send his soul to hell. / Come, lady, I will show thee to my kin; / And they shall say when Richard me begot, / If thou hadst said him nay, it had been sin: / Who says it was, he lies; I say 'twas not.

Now, by this light, if I were to be conceived again, madam, I wouldn't want a better father. Some sins are excused here on earth, and yours is one. Your fault was not foolishness. You had to give your heart to him, a tribute to an all-commanding love, against whose fury and unmatched strength the fearless lion couldn't fight or keep its royal heart from Richard's hand. A man who can rip the hearts out of lions by force can easily win a woman's. Yes, mother, with all my heart I thank you for my father! If any man alive dares to say you did wrong when I was conceived, I'll send his soul to hell. Come, lady, I'll introduce you to my family, and they'll say that if you had refused Richard when he fathered me, that would have been the sin. Whoever says it was a sin is lying; I say it was not.

Before Angiers well met, brave Austria.— / Arthur, that great forerunner of thy blood, / Richard, that robb'd the lion of his heart, / And fought the holy wars in Palestine, / By this brave duke came early to his grave: / And, for amends to his posterity, / At our importance hither is he come / To spread his colours, boy, in thy behalf; / And to rebuke the usurpation / Of thy unnatural uncle, English John: / Embrace him, love him, give him welcome hither.

Well met before Angiers, brave Austria. Arthur, your great ancestor Richard, who tore the heart out of a lion and fought the holy wars in Palestine, was sent early to his grave by this brave duke. Now, to make amends to Richard's family, he has come here at our urging to raise his banners on your behalf, boy, and to punish the usurping of your unnatural uncle, English John. Embrace him, love him, welcome him here.

God shall forgive you Coeur-de-lion's death / The rather that you give his offspring life, / Shadowing their right under your wings of war: / I give you welcome with a powerless hand, / But with a heart full of unstained love,— / Welcome before the gates of Angiers, duke.

God will forgive you for the Lionheart's death all the more readily because you give his family new life, sheltering their right under your wings of war. I welcome you with a powerless hand but with a heart full of pure love. Welcome before the gates of Angiers, duke.
A noble boy! Who would not do thee right?
A noble boy! Who wouldn't fight for your rights?

Upon thy cheek lay I this zealous kiss, / As seal to this indenture of my love,— / That to my home I will no more return, / Till Angiers, and the right thou hast in France, / Together with that pale, that white-fac'd shore, / Whose foot spurns back the ocean's roaring tides, / And coops from other lands her islanders,— / Even till that England, hedg'd in with the main, / That water-walled bulwark, still secure / And confident from foreign purposes,— / Even till that utmost corner of the west / Salute thee for her king: till then, fair boy, / Will I not think of home, but follow arms.

I lay this eager kiss on your cheek as the seal on this contract of my love: that I will never go home until Angiers and your rights in France, together with that pale, white-cliffed shore whose foot kicks back the ocean's roaring tides and shuts its islanders off from other lands, until England, hedged in by the sea, that water-walled fortress, always safe and sure against foreign plots, until that farthest corner of the west hails you as its king. Until then, fair boy, I won't think of home but keep fighting.
O, take his mother's thanks, a widow's thanks, / Till your strong hand shall help to give him strength / To make a more requital to your love!
Oh, take his mother's thanks, a widow's thanks, until your strong hand helps to make him strong enough to repay your love better!
The peace of heaven is theirs that lift their swords / In such a just and charitable war.
Heaven's peace belongs to those who raise their swords in such a just and charitable war.

Well then, to work: our cannon shall be bent / Against the brows of this resisting town.— / Call for our chiefest men of discipline, / To cull the plots of best advantages: / We'll lay before this town our royal bones, / Wade to the market-place in Frenchmen's blood, / But we will make it subject to this boy.

Well then, to work. Our cannon will be aimed at the face of this resisting town. Call our chief military experts to choose the best positions. We'll leave our royal bones before this town and wade to the market place in Frenchmen's blood, but we'll make it submit to this boy.

Stay for an answer to your embassy, / Lest unadvis'd you stain your swords with blood: / My Lord Chatillon may from England bring / That right in peace which here we urge in war; / And then we shall repent each drop of blood / That hot rash haste so indirectly shed.

Wait for an answer to your embassy, or you may rashly stain your swords with blood. Lord Chatillon may bring from England in peace the right we are pressing here by war, and then we'd regret every drop of blood that hot, rash haste had wrongly spilled.
A wonder, lady!—lo, upon thy wish, / Our messenger Chatillon is arriv'd.
A wonder, lady! Look: just as you wished, our messenger Chatillon has arrived.
What England says, say briefly, gentle lord; / We coldly pause for thee; Chatillon, speak.
Tell us briefly what England says, my lord. We wait calmly for you. Chatillon, speak.

Then turn your forces from this paltry siege, / And stir them up against a mightier task. / England, impatient of your just demands, / Hath put himself in arms: the adverse winds, / Whose leisure I have stay'd, have given him time / To land his legions all as soon as I; / His marches are expedient to this town, / His forces strong, his soldiers confident. / With him along is come the mother-queen, / An Ate, stirring him to blood and strife; / With her her neice, the Lady Blanch of Spain; / With them a bastard of the king's deceas'd: / And all the unsettled humours of the land,— / Rash, inconsiderate, fiery voluntaries, / With ladies' faces and fierce dragons' spleens,— / Have sold their fortunes at their native homes, / Bearing their birthrights proudly on their backs, / To make a hazard of new fortunes here. / In brief, a braver choice of dauntless spirits / Than now the English bottoms have waft o'er / Did never float upon the swelling tide / To do offence and scathe in Christendom.

Then turn your forces from this petty siege and rouse them for a greater task. England, angered by your just demands, has taken up arms. The contrary winds that I had to wait for gave him time to land his troops as soon as I did. He is marching quickly to this town; his forces are strong and his soldiers confident. With him comes the Queen Mother, a goddess of discord driving him to blood and strife; with her, her niece, Lady Blanche of Spain; with them, a bastard son of the dead king; and all the restless hotheads of the land, rash, reckless, fiery volunteers with ladies' faces and dragons' tempers, who have sold their estates at home and wear their inheritances proudly on their backs, to gamble on new fortunes here. In short, a finer collection of fearless men than the English ships have now carried over never sailed the swelling sea to do harm and damage in Christendom.
The interruption of their churlish drums / Cuts off more circumstance: they are at hand; / To parley or to fight: therefore prepare.
The sound of their rough drums cuts off further detail. They are here, to talk or fight, so get ready.
How much unlook'd-for is this expedition!
By how much unexpected, by so much / We must awake endeavour for defence; / For courage mounteth with occasion: / Let them be welcome, then; we are prepar'd.
The more unexpected it is, the more we must rouse ourselves for defence, because courage rises to the occasion. So let them come; we are ready.

Peace be to France, if France in peace permit / Our just and lineal entrance to our own! / If not, bleed France, and peace ascend to heaven, / Whiles we, God's wrathful agent, do correct / Their proud contempt that beats his peace to heaven!

Peace to France, if France will peacefully allow our rightful, hereditary entry into what is ours! If not, let France bleed, and peace go up to heaven, while we, as God's angry agent, punish their proud contempt that drives His peace back up to heaven!

Peace be to England, if that war return / From France to England, there to live in peace! / England we love; and for that England's sake / With burden of our armour here we sweat. / This toil of ours should be a work of thine; / But thou from loving England art so far / That thou hast under-wrought his lawful king, / Cut off the sequence of posterity, / Outfaced infant state, and done a rape / Upon the maiden virtue of the crown. / Look here upon thy brother Geffrey's face:— / These eyes, these brows, were moulded out of his: / This little abstract doth contain that large / Which died in Geffrey; and the hand of time / Shall draw this brief into as huge a volume. / That Geffrey was thy elder brother born, / And this his son; England was Geffrey's right, / And this is Geffrey's: in the name of God, / How comes it then, that thou art call'd a king, / When living blood doth in these temples beat, / Which owe the crown that thou o'er-masterest?

Peace to England, if your war goes back from France to England, to live there in peace! We love England, and it's for England's sake that we sweat here under the weight of our armour. This should be your work, but you are so far from loving England that you have undermined its lawful king, cut off the line of succession, defied a child's rights and raped the pure virtue of the crown. Look at your brother Geoffrey's face here: these eyes and brows were moulded from his. This small copy contains the whole that died in Geoffrey, and time will enlarge this summary into as big a volume. Geoffrey was born your elder brother, and this is his son. England was Geoffrey's by right, and this boy is Geoffrey's. In God's name, then, how can you be called a king while living blood beats in these temples that owns the crown you have seized?
From whom hast thou this great commission, France, / To draw my answer from thy articles?
Who gave you this great authority, France, to make me answer to your charges?

From that supernal judge that stirs good thoughts / In any breast of strong authority, / To look into the blots and stains of right. / That judge hath made me guardian to this boy: / Under whose warrant I impeach thy wrong; / And by whose help I mean to chastise it.

That supreme judge in heaven who puts good thoughts into the hearts of the powerful, to examine the blots and stains on justice. That judge has made me this boy's guardian. By His warrant I accuse you of wrong, and with His help I mean to punish it.
Excuse,—it is to beat usurping down.
Excuse me: I am beating down usurping.
Who is it thou dost call usurper, France?
Whom are you calling a usurper, France?
Let me make answer;—thy usurping son.
Let me answer that: your usurping son.
Out, insolent! thy bastard shall be king, / That thou mayst be a queen, and check the world!
Get out, you insolent woman! You want your bastard to be king so that you can be queen and boss the world!

My bed was ever to thy son as true / As thine was to thy husband; and this boy / Liker in feature to his father Geffrey / Than thou and John in manners,—being as like / As rain to water, or devil to his dam. / My boy a bastard! By my soul, I think / His father never was so true begot: / It cannot be, an if thou wert his mother.

My bed was always as faithful to your son as yours was to your husband. This boy is more like his father Geoffrey in looks than you and John are alike in manners, and you two are as alike as rain and water, or the devil and his mother. My boy a bastard! I swear I think his father was never so honestly conceived, not if you were his mother.
There's a good mother, boy, that blots thy father.
There's a good mother, boy, who slanders your father.
There's a good grandam, boy, that would blot thee.
There's a good grandmother, boy, who would slander you.

One that will play the devil, sir, with you, / An 'a may catch your hide and you alone. / You are the hare of whom the proverb goes, / Whose valour plucks dead lions by the beard: / I'll smoke your skin-coat an I catch you right; / Sirrah, look to 't; i' faith I will, i' faith.

One who'll play the devil with you, sir, if he can catch you and your lion's skin alone. You're the hare in the proverb, brave enough to pluck dead lions by the beard. I'll beat your fur coat if I catch you properly. Watch out, sir; I mean it, I mean it.
O, well did he become that lion's robe / That did disrobe the lion of that robe!
Oh, that lion's robe suited the man who stripped the lion of it!
It lies as sightly on the back of him / As great Alcides' shows upon an ass:— / But, ass, I'll take that burden from your back, / Or lay on that shall make your shoulders crack.
It sits as nicely on his back as great Hercules' lion skin would on a donkey. But, donkey, I'll take that load off your back, or put something on it that will make your shoulders crack.
What cracker is this same that deafs our ears / With this abundance of superfluous breath?
What noisy firecracker is this, deafening our ears with all this useless hot air?
Louis, determine what we shall do straight.
Louis, decide straight away what we should do.

Women and fools, break off your conference.— / King John, this is the very sum of all,— / England and Ireland, Anjou, Touraine, Maine, / In right of Arthur, do I claim of thee: / Wilt thou resign them, and lay down thy arms?

Women and fools, stop your chatter. King John, this is the whole of it: in Arthur's right I claim from you England and Ireland, Anjou, Touraine and Maine. Will you give them up and lay down your weapons?
My life as soon:—I do defy thee, France. / Arthur of Bretagne, yield thee to my hand; / And out of my dear love, I'll give thee more / Than e'er the coward hand of France can win: / Submit thee, boy.

I'd as soon give up my life. I defy you, France. Arthur of Brittany, put yourself in my hands, and out of my love I'll give you more than the cowardly hand of France can ever win for you. Submit, boy.
Do, child, go to it' grandam, child; / Give grandam kingdom, and it' grandam will / Give it a plum, a cherry, and a fig. / There's a good grandam!
Yes, child, go to its granny, child. Give granny the kingdom, and its granny will give it a plum, a cherry and a fig. There's a good granny!
Good my mother, peace! / I would that I were low laid in my grave: / I am not worth this coil that's made for me.
Please, mother, be quiet! I wish I were laid deep in my grave. I'm not worth all this fuss being made over me.
His mother shames him so, poor boy, he weeps.
His mother shames him so much, poor boy, that he cries.

Now, shame upon you, whe'er she does or no! / His grandam's wrongs, and not his mother's shames, / Draws those heaven-moving pearls from his poor eyes, / Which heaven shall take in nature of a fee: / Ay, with these crystal beads heaven shall be brib'd / To do him justice, and revenge on you.

Shame on you, whether she does or not! It's his grandmother's wrongs, not his mother's shame, that draw those tears from his poor eyes, tears that would move heaven. Heaven will take them as a fee: yes, heaven will be bribed with these crystal beads to give him justice and take revenge on you.
Thou monstrous slanderer of heaven and earth!
You monstrous slanderer of heaven and earth!

Thou monstrous injurer of heaven and earth! / Call not me slanderer: thou and thine usurp / The dominations, royalties, and rights, / Of this oppressed boy: this is thy eldest son's son, / Infortunate in nothing but in thee: / Thy sins are visited in this poor child; / The canon of the law is laid on him, / Being but the second generation / Removed from thy sin-conceiving womb.

You monstrous wrongdoer against heaven and earth! Don't call me a slanderer. You and your son steal the lands, royal powers and rights of this oppressed boy. He is your eldest son's son, unlucky in nothing except in having you. Your sins are punished in this poor child; the law of the Bible falls on him, though he is only the second generation from your sinful womb.

I have but this to say,— / That he is not only plagued for her sin, / But God hath made her sin and her the plague / On this removed issue, plagu'd for her / And with her plague, her sin; his injury / Her injury,—the beadle to her sin; / All punish'd in the person of this child, / And all for her: a plague upon her!

I have only this to say: he is not only punished for her sin, but God has made her sin and her herself the plague on this descendant. He is punished for her and by her: her sin is his injury, and she is the officer who whips him for her sin. All of it punished in this child, and all because of her. A plague on her!
Thou unadvised scold, I can produce / A will that bars the title of thy son.
You reckless scold, I can produce a will that cancels your son's claim.
Ay, who doubts that? a will, a wicked will; / A woman's will; a canker'd grandam's will!
Yes, who doubts that? A will, a wicked will, a woman's will, a spiteful grandmother's will!

Peace, lady! pause, or be more temperate: / It ill beseems this presence to cry aim / To these ill-tuned repetitions.— / Some trumpet summon hither to the walls / These men of Angiers: let us hear them speak / Whose title they admit, Arthur's or John's.

Quiet, lady! Stop, or be calmer. It doesn't suit this company to egg on these jarring repetitions. Let a trumpet call the men of Angiers to the walls. Let's hear from them whose claim they accept, Arthur's or John's.
Who is it that hath warn'd us to the walls?
Who has called us to the walls?
England for itself:— / You men of Angiers, and my loving subjects,—
England, on its own behalf. You men of Angiers, my loving subjects...
You loving men of Angiers, Arthur's subjects, / Our trumpet call'd you to this gentle parle.
You loving men of Angiers, Arthur's subjects, our trumpet called you to this friendly talk...

For our advantage; therefore hear us first. / These flags of France, that are advanced here / Before the eye and prospect of your town, / Have hither march'd to your endamagement; / The cannons have their bowels full of wrath, / And ready mounted are they to spit forth / Their iron indignation 'gainst your walls: / All preparation for a bloody siege / And merciless proceeding by these French / Confronts your city's eyes, your winking gates; / And, but for our approach, those sleeping stones / That as a waist doth girdle you about, / By the compulsion of their ordinance / By this time from their fixed beds of lime / Had been dishabited, and wide havoc made / For bloody power to rush upon your peace. / But, on the sight of us, your lawful king,— / Who, painfully, with much expedient march, / Have brought a countercheck before your gates, / To save unscratch'd your city's threatn'd cheeks,— / Behold, the French, amaz'd, vouchsafe a parle; / And now, instead of bullets wrapp'd in fire, / To make a shaking fever in your walls, / They shoot but calm words folded up in smoke, / To make a faithless error in your ears: / Which trust accordingly, kind citizens, / And let us in, your king; whose labour'd spirits, / Forwearied in this action of swift speed, / Craves harbourage within your city-walls.

...for our benefit, so hear us first. These French flags, set up here in full view of your town, have marched here to harm you. Their cannons are full of anger and mounted ready to spit iron fury at your walls. All the preparations for a bloody siege and a merciless attack by these French face your city's eyes, your closed gates. If we hadn't come, the sleeping stones that circle you like a belt would by now have been battered from their beds of mortar, and a wide gap made for bloody force to rush in on your peace. But at the sight of us, your lawful king, who with great effort and a fast march have brought a counter-force before your gates to save your city's threatened face from a scratch, look: the astonished French agree to talk. Now, instead of fiery cannonballs to shake your walls with fever, they fire only calm words wrapped in smoke, to trick your ears into disloyalty. Treat them accordingly, kind citizens, and let us in, your king, whose tired spirits, worn out by this rapid campaign, ask for shelter inside your city walls.

When I have said, make answer to us both. / Lo, in this right hand, whose protection / Is most divinely vow'd upon the right / Of him it holds, stands young Plantagenet, / Son to the elder brother of this man, / And king o'er him and all that he enjoys: / For this down-trodden equity we tread / In war-like march these greens before your town; / Being no further enemy to you / Than the constraint of hospitable zeal / In the relief of this oppressed child / Religiously provokes. Be pleased then / To pay that duty which you truly owe / To him that owes it, namely, this young prince: / And then our arms, like to a muzzled bear, / Save in aspect, hath all offence seal'd up; / Our cannons' malice vainly shall be spent / Against the invulnerable clouds of heaven; / And with a blessed and unvex'd retire, / With unhack'd swords and helmets all unbruis'd, / We will bear home that lusty blood again / Which here we came to spout against your town, / And leave your children, wives, and you, in peace. / But if you fondly pass our proffer'd offer, / 'Tis not the roundure of your old-fac'd walls / Can hide you from our messengers of war, / Though all these English, and their discipline, / Were harbour'd in their rude circumference. / Then, tell us, shall your city call us lord / In that behalf which we have challeng'd it? / Or shall we give the signal to our rage, / And stalk in blood to our possession?

When I have spoken, answer us both. Look: in my right hand, whose protection is solemnly sworn to the cause of the one it holds, stands young Plantagenet, son of this man's elder brother and king over him and all he has. For this downtrodden justice we march in arms over these fields before your town. We are no more your enemy than our generous duty to relieve this oppressed child requires. So be pleased to pay the duty you truly owe to its true owner, this young prince. Then our army, like a muzzled bear, will keep only its fierce looks and have all its harm sealed up. Our cannons' malice will be wasted on the clouds of heaven, which can't be hurt, and with a blessed, untroubled retreat, with unnotched swords and undented helmets, we'll carry home the lively blood we came here to spill against your town, and leave your children, wives and you in peace. But if you foolishly ignore our offer, the circle of your ancient walls won't hide you from our messengers of war, even if all these English and their army were sheltered inside it. So tell us: will your city call us lord on the boy's behalf, as we have demanded? Or shall we give our fury the signal and wade through blood to take possession?
In brief: we are the King of England's subjects: / For him, and in his right, we hold this town.
In short: we are subjects of the King of England. We hold this town for him and in his name.
Acknowledge then the king, and let me in.
Then acknowledge your king and let me in.
That can we not; but he that proves the king, / To him will we prove loyal: till that time / Have we ramm'd up our gates against the world.
That we can't do. But whoever proves to be the king, we will prove loyal to him. Until then we have barred our gates against the whole world.
Doth not the crown of England prove the king? / And if not that, I bring you witnesses, / Twice fifteen thousand hearts of England's breed,—
Doesn't the crown of England prove who is king? And if not, I bring you witnesses: thirty thousand hearts of English stock...
To verify our title with their lives.
...to prove our title with their lives.
As many and as well-born bloods as those,—
As many men, and as well born...
Stand in his face, to contradict his claim.
...stand facing him, to contradict his claim.
Till you compound whose right is worthiest, / We for the worthiest hold the right from both.
Until you settle whose right is the stronger, we will keep the right from both of you, for whoever proves stronger.
Then God forgive the sin of all those souls / That to their everlasting residence, / Before the dew of evening fall, shall fleet, / In dreadful trial of our kingdom's king!
Then God forgive the sins of all the souls that will fly to their eternal home before the evening dew falls, in this dreadful test of who is our kingdom's king!
Amen, amen! Mount, knights! To arms!

Saint George, that swinged the dragon, and e'er since / Sits on his horse' back at mine hostess' door, / Teach us some fence!—Sirrah [To AUSTRIA], were I at home, / At your den, sirrah, with your lioness, / I would set an ox-head to your lion's hide, / And make a monster of you.

Saint George, who thrashed the dragon and ever since has sat on his horse on the sign at my landlady's door, teach us some swordplay! (To Austria) You, sir, if I were at home, at your den, with your lioness, I'd put an ox's head on top of your lion skin and make a monster of you.
O, tremble, for you hear the lion roar.
Oh, tremble, for you hear the lion roar.
Up higher to the plain; where we'll set forth / In best appointment all our regiments.
Up higher, to the plain, where we'll set out all our regiments in the best order.
Speed, then, to take advantage of the field.
Hurry then, to take the best positions on the field.
It shall be so;—[To LOUIS] and at the other hill / Command the rest to stand.—God and our right!
So be it. (To Louis) Order the rest to stand at the other hill. God and our right!

You men of Angiers, open wide your gates / And let young Arthur, Duke of Bretagne, in, / Who, by the hand of France, this day hath made / Much work for tears in many an English mother, / Whose sons lie scatter'd on the bleeding ground; / Many a widow's husband grovelling lies, / Coldly embracing the discolour'd earth; / And victory, with little loss, doth play / Upon the dancing banners of the French, / Who are at hand, triumphantly display'd, / To enter conquerors, and to proclaim / Arthur of Bretagne England's king and yours.

You men of Angiers, open your gates wide and let in young Arthur, Duke of Brittany, who by the hand of France today has made many English mothers weep: their sons lie scattered on the bleeding ground. Many a widow's husband lies face down, coldly hugging the bloodstained earth. And victory, at little cost, plays on the dancing banners of the French, who are close by, displayed in triumph, ready to enter as conquerors and proclaim Arthur of Brittany king of England and of you.

Rejoice, you men of Angiers, ring your bells: / King John, your king and England's, doth approach, / Commander of this hot malicious day: / Their armours, that march'd hence so silver-bright, / Hither return all gilt with Frenchmen's blood; / There stuck no plume in any English crest / That is removed by a staff of France, / Our colours do return in those same hands / That did display them when we first march'd forth; / And, like a jolly troop of huntsmen, come / Our lusty English, all with purpled hands, / Dy'd in the dying slaughter of their foes: / Open your gates and give the victors way.

Rejoice, men of Angiers, ring your bells! King John, your king and England's, is coming, the master of this hot and bitter day. Their armour, which marched out so silver-bright, comes back gilded with Frenchmen's blood. No plume on any English helmet has been knocked off by a French spear. Our flags come back in the same hands that unfurled them when we first marched out, and like a jolly band of huntsmen our strong English come, all with purple hands, dyed in the killing of their enemies. Open your gates and let the winners in.

Heralds, from off our towers, we might behold, / From first to last, the onset and retire / Of both your armies; whose equality / By our best eyes cannot be censured: / Blood hath bought blood, and blows have answer'd blows; / Strength match'd with strength, and power confronted power: / Both are alike, and both alike we like. / One must prove greatest: while they weigh so even, / We hold our town for neither; yet for both.

Heralds, from our towers we could watch your two armies' attack and retreat from start to finish, and our best eyes can't judge between them. Blood has paid for blood, and blows have answered blows; strength has matched strength and power faced power. Both are equal, and we like both equally. One must prove the greater. While they weigh so evenly, we hold our town for neither, and yet for both.

France, hast thou yet more blood to cast away? / Say, shall the current of our right run on? / Whose passage, vex'd with thy impediment, / Shall leave his native channel, and o'erswell / With course disturb'd even thy confining shores, / Unless thou let his silver water keep / A peaceful progress to the ocean.

France, do you have more blood to throw away? Tell me, will the river of our right flow on? If your obstacle blocks it, it will leave its natural channel and flood, in its disturbed course, even over your shores, unless you let its silver water flow peacefully to the ocean.

England, thou hast not sav'd one drop of blood / In this hot trial, more than we of France; / Rather, lost more: and by this hand I swear, / That sways the earth this climate overlooks, / Before we will lay down our just-borne arms, / We'll put thee down, 'gainst whom these arms we bear, / Or add a royal number to the dead, / Gracing the scroll that tells of this war's loss / With slaughter coupled to the name of kings.

England, you haven't saved one drop of blood in this hot contest more than we French have; you've lost more. And by this hand, which rules the land under this sky, I swear that before we lay down the arms we rightly carry, we'll bring you down, against whom we carry them, or add a king to the dead, honouring the list of this war's losses with the name of a king among the slaughtered.

Ha, majesty! how high thy glory towers / When the rich blood of kings is set on fire! / O, now doth Death line his dead chaps with steel; / The swords of soldiers are his teeth, his fangs; / And now he feasts, mousing the flesh of men, / In undetermin'd differences of kings.— / Why stand these royal fronts amazed thus? / Cry, havoc, kings! back to the stained field, / You equal potents, fiery-kindled spirits! / Then let confusion of one part confirm / The other's peace: till then, blows, blood, and death!

Ha, majesty! How high your glory soars when the rich blood of kings is set on fire! Oh, now Death lines his jaws with steel; soldiers' swords are his teeth and fangs, and now he feasts, tearing at men's flesh like a cat at a mouse, over the unsettled quarrels of kings. Why do these royal faces stand there so dazed? Cry "No mercy," kings! Back to the bloody field, you equal powers, you fiery spirits! Let the destruction of one side secure the other's peace. Until then: blows, blood and death!
Whose party do the townsmen yet admit?
Whose side do the townsmen accept now?
Speak, citizens, for England; who's your king?
Speak, citizens: for England, who is your king?
The King of England, when we know the king.
The King of England, when we know who the king is.
Know him in us, that here hold up his right.
Know him in us, who uphold his right here.
In us, that are our own great deputy, / And bear possession of our person here; / Lord of our presence, Angiers, and of you.
In us, who are our own great deputy and present here in person: lord of ourselves, of Angiers and of you.

A greater power than we denies all this; / And till it be undoubted, we do lock / Our former scruple in our strong-barr'd gates; / King'd of our fears, until our fears, resolv'd, / Be by some certain king purg'd and depos'd.

A greater power than ours denies all this. Until it is beyond doubt, we lock our old doubts behind our strongly barred gates, ruled by our fears until some certain king settles those fears and removes them.

By heaven, these scroyles of Angiers flout you, kings, / And stand securely on their battlements / As in a theatre, whence they gape and point / At your industrious scenes and acts of death. / Your royal presences be rul'd by me:— / Do like the mutines of Jerusalem, / Be friends awhile, and both conjointly bend / Your sharpest deeds of malice on this town: / By east and west let France and England mount / Their battering cannon, charged to the mouths, / Till their soul-fearing clamours have brawl'd down / The flinty ribs of this contemptuous city: / I'd play incessantly upon these jades, / Even till unfenced desolation / Leave them as naked as the vulgar air. / That done, dissever your united strengths, / And part your mingled colours once again: / Turn face to face, and bloody point to point; / Then, in a moment, fortune shall cull forth / Out of one side her happy minion, / To whom in favour she shall give the day, / And kiss him with a glorious victory. / How like you this wild counsel, mighty states? / Smacks it not something of the policy?

By heaven, these scabby wretches of Angiers are mocking you, kings. They stand safe on their battlements as if in a theatre, gaping and pointing at your busy scenes and acts of death. Let your royal highnesses take my advice. Do what the rebel factions in Jerusalem did: be friends for a while, and together turn your fiercest attacks on this town. Let France and England set up their battering cannon east and west, loaded to the mouths, until their terrifying roar has knocked down the stony ribs of this scornful city. I'd pound these nags without stopping until defenceless ruin leaves them as naked as the open air. Once that's done, split up your joined forces and separate your mixed flags again. Turn face to face and bloody sword-point to sword-point. Then, in a moment, Fortune will pick out her lucky favourite from one side, give him the day and kiss him with a glorious victory. How do you like this wild advice, mighty rulers? Doesn't it taste a little of statecraft?
Now, by the sky that hangs above our heads, / I like it well.—France, shall we knit our powers, / And lay this Angiers even with the ground; / Then, after, fight who shall be king of it?
Now, by the sky above our heads, I like it. France, shall we join our forces and flatten this Angiers, and then fight over who will be its king?

An if thou hast the mettle of a king,— / Being wrong'd, as we are, by this peevish town,— / Turn thou the mouth of thy artillery, / As we will ours, against these saucy walls; / And when that we have dash'd them to the ground, / Why then defy each other, and, pell-mell, / Make work upon ourselves, for heaven or hell!

If you have the spirit of a king, wronged as we are by this stubborn town, turn the mouths of your guns, as we will ours, against these insolent walls. When we have knocked them to the ground, then defy each other and fight it out in a free-for-all, for heaven or hell!
Let it be so.—Say, where will you assault?
So be it. Tell me, where will you attack?
We from the west will send destruction / Into this city's bosom.
We'll send destruction into the city's heart from the west.
Our thunder from the south / Shall rain their drift of bullets on this town.
Our thunder from the south will rain its storm of cannonballs on this town.
O prudent discipline! From north to south,— / Austria and France shoot in each other's mouth: / I'll stir them to it.[Aside]—Come, away, away!
(Aside) Oh, wise tactics! From north and south, Austria and France will shoot into each other's mouths. I'll encourage them. (Aloud) Come on, away, away!

Hear us, great kings: vouchsafe awhile to stay, / And I shall show you peace and fair-fac'd league; / Win you this city without stroke or wound; / Rescue those breathing lives to die in beds / That here come sacrifices for the field: / Persever not, but hear me, mighty kings.

Listen to us, great kings. Please wait a little, and I'll show you peace and a fair alliance. You'll win this city without a blow or a wound, and save these living men, who came here as sacrifices to the battlefield, to die in their beds. Don't press on, but hear me, mighty kings.
Speak on with favour; we are bent to hear.
Speak on; you have our leave. We are ready to listen.

That daughter there of Spain, the Lady Blanch, / Is niece to England:—look upon the years / Of Louis the Dauphin and that lovely maid: / If lusty love should go in quest of beauty, / Where should he find it fairer than in Blanch? / If zealous love should go in search of virtue, / Where should he find it purer than in Blanch? / If love ambitious sought a match of birth, / Whose veins bound richer blood than Lady Blanch? / Such as she is, in beauty, virtue, birth, / Is the young Dauphin every way complete,— / If not complete of, say he is not she; / And she again wants nothing, to name want, / If want it be not, that she is not he: / He is the half part of a blessed man, / Left to be finished by such a she; / And she a fair divided excellence, / Whose fulness of perfection lies in him. / O, two such silver currents, when they join / Do glorify the banks that bound them in; / And two such shores to two such streams made one, / Two such controlling bounds, shall you be, kings, / To these two princes, if you marry them. / This union shall do more than battery can / To our fast-closed gates; for at this match, / With swifter spleen than powder can enforce, / The mouth of passage shall we fling wide ope, / And give you entrance; but without this match, / The sea enraged is not half so deaf, / Lions more confident, mountains and rocks / More free from motion; no, not Death himself / In mortal fury half so peremptory / As we to keep this city.

That daughter of Spain there, Lady Blanche, is the King of England's niece. Look at the ages of Louis the Dauphin and that lovely girl. If passionate love went looking for beauty, where would it find it fairer than in Blanche? If devoted love went looking for virtue, where would it find it purer than in Blanche? If ambitious love wanted a match of noble birth, whose veins hold richer blood than Lady Blanche's? Just as she is in beauty, virtue and birth, the young Dauphin is complete in every way. If he's incomplete, it's only that he isn't her; and she lacks nothing, if it is a lack, except that she isn't him. He is half of a blessed man, waiting to be completed by such a woman, and she is a fair, divided excellence whose perfection is completed in him. Oh, when two such silver streams join, they glorify the banks that hold them in. And you kings will be two such banks to two such streams made one, two such guiding shores to these two princes, if you marry them. This union will do more than cannon could against our firmly shut gates. At this match we'll throw open the entrance quicker than gunpowder could force it, and let you in. But without this match the raging sea isn't half so deaf, lions half so bold, mountains and rocks so unmovable, no, not even Death himself in deadly fury half so determined, as we are to keep this city.

Here's a stay / That shakes the rotten carcase of old Death / Out of his rags! Here's a large mouth, indeed, / That spits forth death and mountains, rocks and seas; / Talks as familiarly of roaring lions / As maids of thirteen do of puppy-dogs! / What cannoneer begot this lusty blood? / He speaks plain cannon,—fire and smoke and bounce; / He gives the bastinado with his tongue; / Our ears are cudgell'd; not a word of his / But buffets better than a fist of France. / Zounds! I was never so bethump'd with words / Since I first call'd my brother's father dad.

Here's an obstacle that shakes old Death's rotten body out of its rags! Here's a big mouth indeed, that spits out death and mountains, rocks and seas, and talks about roaring lions as casually as thirteen-year-old girls talk about puppies! What gunner fathered this lively fellow? He speaks pure cannon: fire, smoke and bang. He beats you with his tongue; our ears are clubbed. Every word of his hits harder than a French fist. Damn it! I've never been so thumped with words since I first called my brother's father "Dad".

Son, list to this conjunction, make this match; / Give with our niece a dowry large enough; / For by this knot thou shalt so surely tie / Thy now unsur'd assurance to the crown, / That yon green boy shall have no sun to ripe / The bloom that promiseth a mighty fruit. / I see a yielding in the looks of France; / Mark how they whisper: urge them while their souls / Are capable of this ambition, / Lest zeal, now melted by the windy breath / Of soft petitions, pity, and remorse, / Cool and congeal again to what it was.

Son, listen to this proposal; make this match. Give our niece a big enough dowry, because this knot will tie your still uncertain hold on the crown so firmly that that green boy will have no sun to ripen the blossom that promises such a mighty fruit. I see France is giving way; look how they whisper. Press them while their minds are open to this ambition, before their zeal, now softened by the windy breath of gentle pleas, pity and compassion, cools and hardens again into what it was.
Why answer not the double majesties / This friendly treaty of our threaten'd town?
Why don't the two majesties answer this friendly offer from our threatened town?
Speak England first, that hath been forward first / To speak unto this city: what say you?
England speak first, since you were first to address this city. What do you say?

If that the Dauphin there, thy princely son, / Can in this book of beauty read 'I love,' / Her dowry shall weigh equal with a queen; / For Anjou, and fair Touraine, Maine, Poictiers, / And all that we upon this side the sea,— / Except this city now by us besieg'd,— / Find liable to our crown and dignity, / Shall gild her bridal bed; and make her rich / In titles, honours, and promotions, / As she in beauty, education, blood, / Holds hand with any princess of the world.

If the Dauphin there, your royal son, can read "I love" in this book of beauty, her dowry will equal a queen's. Anjou, fair Touraine, Maine, Poitiers, and everything on this side of the sea, except this city we are now besieging, that belongs to our crown and rank, will gild her wedding bed and make her as rich in titles, honours and rank as she is equal to any princess in the world in beauty, upbringing and blood.
What say'st thou, boy? look in the lady's face.
What do you say, boy? Look in the lady's face.

I do, my lord, and in her eye I find / A wonder, or a wondrous miracle, / The shadow of myself form'd in her eye; / Which, being but the shadow of your son, / Becomes a sun, and makes your son a shadow: / I do protest I never lov'd myself / Till now infixed I beheld myself / Drawn in the flattering table of her eye.

I am, my lord, and in her eye I find a wonder, a wonderful miracle: a reflection of myself in her eye. Though only your son's reflection, it becomes a sun and makes your son a shadow. I swear I never loved myself until now, when I saw myself fixed there, painted in the flattering picture of her eye.

[Aside] Drawn in the flattering table of her eye!— / Hang'd in the frowning wrinkle of her brow, / And quarter'd in her heart!—he doth espy / Himself love's traitor! This is pity now, / That, hang'd, and drawn, and quarter'd, there should be / In such a love so vile a lout as he.

(Aside) "Painted in the flattering picture of her eye"! Hanged in the frown of her brow and quartered in her heart! He sees himself as love's traitor. What a pity that in such a love there should be so vile a lout to be hanged, drawn and quartered.

My uncle's will in this respect is mine. / If he see aught in you that makes him like, / That anything he sees, which moves his liking / I can with ease translate it to my will; / Or if you will, to speak more properly, / I will enforce it easily to my love. / Further, I will not flatter you, my lord, / That all I see in you is worthy love, / Than this,—that nothing do I see in you, / Though churlish thoughts themselves should be your judge,— / That I can find should merit any hate.

My uncle's will in this is mine. If he sees anything in you that he likes, I can easily turn whatever he likes into my own will, or, to put it more properly, if you like, I can easily make myself love it. Beyond that, my lord, I won't flatter you by saying everything I see in you is worth loving. I'll only say this: I see nothing in you, even if the meanest thoughts were judging you, that deserves any hate.
What say these young ones?—What say you, my niece?
What do these young people say? What do you say, my niece?
That she is bound in honour still to do / What you in wisdom still vouchsafe to say.
That she is bound in honour always to do whatever you in your wisdom decide.
Speak then, Prince Dauphin; can you love this lady?
Then speak, Prince Dauphin. Can you love this lady?
Nay, ask me if I can refrain from love; / For I do love her most unfeignedly.
Ask me rather if I can stop myself loving, for I love her with all sincerity.

Then do I give Volquessen, Touraine, Maine, / Poictiers, and Anjou, these five provinces, / With her to thee; and this addition more, / Full thirty thousand marks of English coin.— / Philip of France, if thou be pleas'd withal, / Command thy son and daughter to join hands.

Then with her I give you Vexin, Touraine, Maine, Poitiers and Anjou, these five provinces, and in addition a full thirty thousand marks in English money. Philip of France, if you are pleased with this, tell your son and daughter to join hands.
It likes us well.—Young princes, close your hands.
We like it well. Young prince and princess, join hands.
And your lips too; for I am well assur'd / That I did so when I was first assur'd.
And lips too, because I'm sure I did that when I was first engaged.

Now, citizens of Angiers, ope your gates, / Let in that amity which you have made; / For at Saint Mary's chapel presently / The rites of marriage shall be solemniz'd.— / Is not the Lady Constance in this troop? / I know she is not; for this match made up / Her presence would have interrupted much: / Where is she and her son? tell me, who knows.

Now, citizens of Angiers, open your gates and let in the friendship you have made, because the marriage will be held straight away at Saint Mary's chapel. Is Lady Constance not in this group? I know she isn't, because her presence would have got in the way of this match. Where are she and her son? Tell me, whoever knows.
She is sad and passionate at your highness' tent.
She is in your highness's tent, sad and upset.

And, by my faith, this league that we have made / Will give her sadness very little cure.— / Brother of England, how may we content / This widow lady? In her right we came; / Which we, God knows, have turn'd another way, / To our own vantage.

And truly, this alliance we've made won't cure her sadness much. Brother of England, how can we satisfy this widow? We came here to fight for her right, and God knows we have turned it to our own advantage.

We will heal up all; / For we'll create young Arthur Duke of Bretagne, / And Earl of Richmond; and this rich fair town / We make him lord of.—Call the Lady Constance: / Some speedy messenger bid her repair / To our solemnity:—I trust we shall, / If not fill up the measure of her will, / Yet in some measure satisfy her so / That we shall stop her exclamation. / Go we, as well as haste will suffer us, / To this unlook'd-for, unprepared pomp.

We'll heal everything. We'll make young Arthur Duke of Brittany and Earl of Richmond, and make him lord of this rich, fair town. Call Lady Constance; send a fast messenger to bid her come to our ceremony. I trust that if we don't satisfy all she wants, we'll satisfy her enough to stop her complaints. Let's go, as fast as we can manage, to this unexpected, unprepared celebration.

Mad world! mad kings! mad composition! / John, to stop Arthur's title in the whole, / Hath willingly departed with a part; / And France,—whose armour conscience buckled on, / Whom zeal and charity brought to the field / As God's own soldier,—rounded in the ear / With that same purpose-changer, that sly devil; / That broker, that still breaks the pate of faith; / That daily break-vow, he that wins of all, / Of kings, of beggars, old men, young men, maids,— / Who having no external thing to lose / But the word maid, cheats the poor maid of that; / That smooth-fac'd gentleman, tickling commodity,— / Commodity, the bias of the world; / The world, who of itself is peised well, / Made to run even upon even ground, / Till this advantage, this vile-drawing bias, / This sway of motion, this commodity, / Makes it take head from all indifferency, / From all direction, purpose, course, intent: / And this same bias, this commodity, / This bawd, this broker, this all-changing word, / Clapp'd on the outward eye of fickle France, / Hath drawn him from his own determin'd aid, / From a resolv'd and honourable war, / To a most base and vile-concluded peace.— / And why rail I on this commodity? / But for because he hath not woo'd me yet: / Not that I have the power to clutch my hand / When his fair angels would salute my palm; / But for my hand, as unattempted yet, / Like a poor beggar, raileth on the rich. / Well, whiles I am a beggar, I will rail, / And say, There is no sin but to be rich; / And being rich, my virtue then shall be, / To say, There is no vice but beggary: / Since kings break faith upon commodity, / Gain, be my lord!—for I will worship thee.

Mad world! Mad kings! Mad deal! John, to stop Arthur claiming the whole, has willingly given away a part. And France, whose armour was buckled on by conscience, whom zeal and charity brought to the battlefield as God's own soldier, has had his ear whispered into by that same changer of purposes, that sly devil, that go-between who always breaks the head of good faith, that daily vow-breaker who wins out over everyone, kings, beggars, old men, young men, girls, and cheats the poor girl who has nothing to lose but the name of virgin out of even that: that smooth-faced, flattering gentleman, Self-Interest. Self-Interest, the weight that pulls the world off course. The world is well balanced in itself, made to roll straight on level ground, until this advantage, this vile pulling weight, this swerve, this Self-Interest makes it veer away from all fairness, from every direction, purpose, course and aim. And this same weight, this Self-Interest, this pimp, this dealer, this word that changes everything, set before fickle France's eye, has drawn him from the help he had resolved to give, from a determined and honourable war, to a most low and shamefully settled peace. And why do I rail against Self-Interest? Only because he hasn't courted me yet. Not that I'd have the strength to keep my hand closed when his lovely gold coins came to greet my palm; but my hand, not yet tempted, rails against the rich like a poor beggar. Well, while I'm a beggar I'll rail and say the only sin is being rich, and when I'm rich my virtue will be to say the only vice is being poor. Since kings break their word for Self-Interest, Profit, be my lord, for I will worship you!

Gone to be married! gone to swear a peace! / False blood to false blood join'd! gone to be friends! / Shall Louis have Blanch? and Blanch those provinces? / It is not so; thou hast misspoke, misheard; / Be well advis'd, tell o'er thy tale again: / It cannot be; thou dost but say 'tis so; / I trust I may not trust thee; for thy word / Is but the vain breath of a common man: / Believe me, I do not believe thee, man; / I have a king's oath to the contrary. / Thou shalt be punish'd for thus frighting me, / For I am sick and capable of fears; / Oppress'd with wrongs, and therefore full of fears; / A widow, husbandless, subject to fears; / A woman, naturally born to fears; / And though thou now confess thou didst but jest, / With my vex'd spirits I cannot take a truce, / But they will quake and tremble all this day. / What dost thou mean by shaking of thy head? / Why dost thou look so sadly on my son? / What means that hand upon that breast of thine? / Why holds thine eye that lamentable rheum, / Like a proud river peering o'er his bounds? / Be these sad signs confirmers of thy words? / Then speak again,—not all thy former tale, / But this one word, whether thy tale be true.

Gone to be married! Gone to swear a peace! False blood joined to false blood! Gone to be friends! Will Louis have Blanche, and Blanche those provinces? It isn't so. You've misspoken, misheard. Think carefully and tell your story again. It can't be; you only say it is. I trust I can't trust you, because your word is only the empty breath of a common man. Believe me, I don't believe you, man. I have a king's oath to the contrary. You'll be punished for frightening me like this, because I am sick and prone to fears, weighed down with wrongs and so full of fears, a widow with no husband, open to fears, a woman, born by nature to fears. And even if you now confess you were only joking, I can't make a truce with my troubled spirits; they will shake and tremble all day long. What do you mean by shaking your head? Why do you look so sadly at my son? What does that hand on your chest mean? Why are your eyes full of those pitiful tears, like a swollen river rising over its banks? Are these sad signs confirming your words? Then speak again: not your whole story, just this one word, whether your story is true.
As true as I believe you think them false / That give you cause to prove my saying true.
As true as I believe you think those people false who give you reason to prove what I say is true.

O, if thou teach me to believe this sorrow, / Teach thou this sorrow how to make me die; / And let belief and life encounter so / As doth the fury of two desperate men, / Which in the very meeting fall and die!— / Louis marry Blanch! O boy, then where art thou? / France friend with England! what becomes of me?— / Fellow, be gone: I cannot brook thy sight; / This news hath made thee a most ugly man.

Oh, if you teach me to believe this sorrow, teach this sorrow how to kill me, and let belief and life meet like the fury of two desperate men who fall and die at the very moment they meet! Louis marry Blanche! Oh, boy, then where does that leave you? France friends with England! What becomes of me? Fellow, go away. I can't stand the sight of you; this news has made you a very ugly man.
What other harm have I, good lady, done, / But spoke the harm that is by others done?
What other harm have I done, good lady, except tell of the harm others have done?
Which harm within itself so heinous is, / As it makes harmful all that speak of it.
That harm is so wicked in itself that it makes everyone who speaks of it harmful.
I do beseech you, madam, be content.

If thou, that bid'st me be content, wert grim, / Ugly, and slanderous to thy mother's womb, / Full of unpleasing blots and sightless stains, / Lame, foolish, crooked, swart, prodigious, / Patch'd with foul moles and eye-offending marks, / I would not care, I then would be content; / For then I should not love thee; no, nor thou / Become thy great birth, nor deserve a crown. / But thou art fair; and at thy birth, dear boy, / Nature and fortune join'd to make thee great: / Of nature's gifts thou mayst with lilies boast, / And with the half-blown rose; but Fortune, O! / She is corrupted, chang'd, and won from thee; / She adulterates hourly with thine uncle John; / And with her golden hand hath pluck'd on France / To tread down fair respect of sovereignty, / And made his majesty the bawd to theirs. / France is a bawd to Fortune and king John— / That strumpet Fortune, that usurping John!— / Tell me, thou fellow, is not France forsworn? / Envenom him with words; or get thee gone, / And leave those woes alone, which I alone / Am bound to under-bear.

If you, who tell me to be calm, were grim, ugly, a disgrace to your mother's womb, full of unpleasant blemishes and ugly stains, lame, foolish, crooked, dark, monstrous, patched with foul moles and eye-offending marks, I wouldn't care; then I would be calm, because then I wouldn't love you, and you wouldn't suit your great birth or deserve a crown. But you are beautiful, and at your birth, dear boy, Nature and Fortune joined to make you great. Of Nature's gifts you can boast like lilies and the half-opened rose. But Fortune, oh! She has been corrupted, changed and won away from you. She commits adultery every hour with your uncle John, and with her golden hand she has lured France to trample on the respect due to rightful kingship and made his majesty a pimp for theirs. France is a pimp for Fortune and King John: that whore Fortune, that usurping John! Tell me, fellow, hasn't France broken his oath?
