Arm yourself against your other enemies. I'll make peace between your soul and you. Young Arthur is alive. This hand of mine is still a virgin, innocent hand, not painted with crimson spots of blood. The dreadful impulse of a murderous thought has never yet entered this heart, and you have slandered nature in my looks, which, however rough outside, still cover a mind too good to butcher an innocent child.

Doth Arthur live? O, haste thee to the peers, / Throw this report on their incensed rage, / And make them tame to their obedience! / Forgive the comment that my passion made / Upon thy feature; for my rage was blind, / And foul imaginary eyes of blood / Presented thee more hideous than thou art. / O, answer not; but to my closet bring / The angry lords with all expedient haste: / I conjure thee but slowly; run more fast.

Is Arthur alive? Oh, hurry to the lords. Throw this news on their burning anger and tame them back to obedience! Forgive what my passion said about your looks, because my rage was blind, and imagined, bloody eyes showed you to me as more hideous than you are. Oh, don't answer, but bring the angry lords to my private room as quickly as you can. I'm urging you too slowly; run faster.

The wall is high, and yet will I leap down:— / Good ground, be pitiful and hurt me not!— / There's few or none do know me: if they did, / This ship-boy's semblance hath disguis'd me quite. / I am afraid; and yet I'll venture it. / If I get down, and do not break my limbs, / I'll find a thousand shifts to get away: / As good to die and go, as die and stay.

The wall is high, and yet I'll jump down. Good ground, be merciful and don't hurt me! Few or no people know me here, and if they did, this ship-boy's disguise hides me completely. I'm afraid, and yet I'll risk it. If I get down without breaking my limbs, I'll find a thousand ways to escape. Better to die trying to go than die staying.
O me! my uncle's spirit is in these stones:— / Heaven take my soul, and England keep my bones!
Oh no! My uncle's spirit is in these stones. Heaven take my soul, and England keep my bones!
Lords, I will meet him at Saint Edmunds-Bury; / It is our safety, and we must embrace / This gentle offer of the perilous time.
Lords, I'll meet him at Saint Edmundsbury. It means our safety, and we must accept this kind offer in these dangerous times.
Who brought that letter from the cardinal?
Who brought that letter from the cardinal?
The Count Melun, a noble lord of France, / Whose private with me of the Dauphin's love / Is much more general than these lines import.
Count Melun, a noble French lord, whose private assurance to me of the Dauphin's friendship goes much further than these lines say.
To-morrow morning let us meet him then.
Then let's meet him tomorrow morning.
Or rather then set forward; for 'twill be / Two long days' journey, lords, or e'er we meet.
Or rather set out then, because it will be two long days' journey, lords, before we meet.
Once more to-day well met, distemper'd lords! / The king by me requests your presence straight.
Well met again today, angry lords! The King asks through me for your presence at once.

The King hath dispossess'd himself of us. / We will not line his thin bestained cloak / With our pure honours, nor attend the foot / That leaves the print of blood where'er it walks. / Return and tell him so: we know the worst.
The King has thrown us off. We won't line his thin, stained cloak with our pure honours, or follow the foot that leaves a bloody print wherever it walks. Go back and tell him so. We know the worst.
Whate'er you think, good words, I think, were best.
Whatever you think, good words would be best, I think.
Our griefs, and not our manners, reason now.
Our grievances, not our manners, are doing the reasoning now.
But there is little reason in your grief; / Therefore 'twere reason you had manners now.
But there is little reason in your grievances, so it would be reasonable for you to show some manners now.
Sir, sir, impatience hath his privilege.
Sir, sir, anger has its privileges.
'Tis true,—to hurt his master, no man else.
True: to hurt its own master, and nobody else.
This is the prison:—what is he lies here?
This is the prison. Who's this lying here?
O death, made proud with pure and princely beauty! / The earth had not a hole to hide this deed.
Oh, Death, made proud with pure and princely beauty! The earth didn't have a hole to hide this deed in.
Murder, as hating what himself hath done, / Doth lay it open to urge on revenge.
Murder, as if hating what it has done, lays it out in the open to spur on revenge.
Or, when he doom'd this beauty to a grave, / Found it too precious-princely for a grave.
Or, when it condemned this beauty to a grave, found it too precious and princely for a grave.

Sir Richard, what think you? Have you beheld, / Or have you read or heard, or could you think? / Or do you almost think, although you see, / That you do see? could thought, without this object, / Form such another? This is the very top, / The height, the crest, or crest unto the crest, / Of murder's arms: this is the bloodiest shame, / The wildest savagery, the vilest stroke, / That ever wall-ey'd wrath or staring rage / Presented to the tears of soft remorse.

Sir Richard, what do you think? Have you ever seen, or read, or heard, or could you imagine, or can you almost believe even though you see it, that you are seeing this? Could the mind, without this sight before it, invent another like it? This is the very peak, the height, the crest, the crest upon the crest of murder's coat of arms. This is the bloodiest shame, the wildest savagery, the vilest blow that glaring anger or wild-eyed rage ever offered to the tears of tender pity.

All murders past do stand excus'd in this; / And this, so sole and so unmatchable, / Shall give a holiness, a purity, / To the yet unbegotten sin of times; / And prove a deadly bloodshed but a jest, / Exampled by this heinous spectacle.

All past murders are excused by this one. And this, so unique and unmatched, will make the sins of future ages, not yet conceived, seem holy and pure, and make deadly bloodshed seem only a joke compared with this terrible sight.
It is a damned and a bloody work; / The graceless action of a heavy hand,— / If that it be the work of any hand.
It is a damned and bloody piece of work, the wicked act of a cruel hand, if it is the work of any hand.

If that it be the work of any hand?— / We had a kind of light what would ensue. / It is the shameful work of Hubert's hand; / The practice and the purpose of the king:— / From whose obedience I forbid my soul, / Kneeling before this ruin of sweet life, / And breathing to his breathless excellence / The incense of a vow, a holy vow, / Never to taste the pleasures of the world, / Never to be infected with delight, / Nor conversant with ease and idleness, / Till I have set a glory to this hand, / By giving it the worship of revenge.

"If it is the work of any hand"? We had some idea of what would happen. It is the shameful work of Hubert's hand, the plot and purpose of the King. I forbid my soul to obey him. Kneeling before this ruin of a sweet life, and breathing to his breathless excellence the incense of a vow, a holy vow: never to taste the pleasures of the world, never to be touched by delight, nor to know ease and idleness, until I have brought glory to this hand by giving it the honour of revenge.
Our souls religiously confirm thy words.
Our souls solemnly confirm your words.
Lords, I am hot with haste in seeking you: / Arthur doth live; the king hath sent for you.
Lords, I'm hot with hurrying to find you. Arthur is alive; the King has sent for you.
O, he is bold, and blushes not at death:— / Avaunt, thou hateful villain, get thee gone!
Oh, he is bold, and doesn't blush in the face of death! Away, you hateful villain, get out!
Must I cheat the law of its work?
Your sword is bright, sir; put it up again.
Your sword is bright, sir. Put it away again.
Not till I sheathe it in a murderer's skin.
Not until I sheathe it in a murderer's skin.

Stand back, Lord Salisbury,—stand back, I say; / By heaven, I think my sword's as sharp as yours: / I would not have you, lord, forget yourself, / Nor tempt the danger of my true defence; / Lest I, by marking of your rage, forget / Your worth, your greatness, and nobility.

Stand back, Lord Salisbury, stand back, I say. By heaven, I think my sword is as sharp as yours. I wouldn't want you, my lord, to forget yourself or risk the danger of my honest self-defence, in case, seeing your rage, I forget your worth, your greatness and your nobility.
Out, dunghill! dar'st thou brave a nobleman?
Get out, you dunghill! Do you dare defy a nobleman?
Not for my life: but yet I dare defend / My innocent life against an emperor.
Not for my life. But I dare defend my innocent life against an emperor.
Do not prove me so; / Yet I am none: whose tongue soe'er speaks false, / Not truly speaks; who speaks not truly, lies.
Don't make me one. I am not one yet. Whoever speaks falsely isn't telling the truth, and whoever doesn't tell the truth lies.
Stand by, or I shall gall you, Falconbridge.
Stand aside, or I'll hurt you, Falconbridge.

Thou wert better gall the devil, Salisbury: / If thou but frown on me, or stir thy foot, / Or teach thy hasty spleen to do me shame, / I'll strike thee dead. Put up thy sword betime: / Or I'll so maul you and your toasting-iron / That you shall think the devil is come from hell.

You'd do better to hurt the devil, Salisbury. If you so much as frown at me, or move your foot, or let your hot temper insult me, I'll strike you dead. Put your sword away in time, or I'll batter you and your toasting fork so badly you'll think the devil has come up from hell.
What wilt thou do, renowned Falconbridge? / Second a villain and a murderer?
What are you doing, famous Falconbridge? Backing a villain and a murderer?
Lord Bigot, I am not one.
'Tis not an hour since I left him well: / I honour'd him, I lov'd him, and will weep / My date of life out for his sweet life's loss.
It's not an hour since I left him well. I honoured him, I loved him, and I'll weep away the rest of my life for the loss of his sweet life.

Trust not those cunning waters of his eyes, / For villainy is not without such rheum; / And he, long traded in it, makes it seem / Like rivers of remorse and innocency. / Away with me, all you whose souls abhor / Th' uncleanly savours of a slaughter-house; / For I am stifled with this smell of sin.

Don't trust those cunning tears of his, because villainy is never short of such water, and he, long practised in it, makes it look like rivers of remorse and innocence. Come away with me, all of you whose souls hate the foul smell of a slaughterhouse, because I'm choked by this stench of sin.
Away toward Bury, to the Dauphin there!
Away towards Bury, to the Dauphin there!
There tell the king he may inquire us out.
Tell the King he can look for us there.
Here's a good world!—Knew you of this fair work? / Beyond the infinite and boundless reach / Of mercy, if thou didst this deed of death, / Art thou damn'd, Hubert.
Here's a fine world! Did you know about this fine piece of work? If you did this deed of death, Hubert, you are damned beyond the infinite, boundless reach of mercy.

Ha! I'll tell thee what; / Thou'rt damn'd as black—nay, nothing is so black; / Thou art more deep damn'd than Prince Lucifer: / There is not yet so ugly a fiend of hell / As thou shalt be, if thou didst kill this child.

Ha! I'll tell you what: you are damned as black... no, nothing is so black. You are more deeply damned than Prince Lucifer. There isn't yet a fiend in hell as ugly as you will be if you killed this child.

If thou didst but consent / To this most cruel act, do but despair; / And if thou want'st a cord, the smallest thread / That ever spider twisted from her womb / Will serve to strangle thee; a rush will be a beam / To hang thee on; or wouldst thou drown thyself, / Put but a little water in a spoon / And it shall be as all the ocean, / Enough to stifle such a villain up. / I do suspect thee very grievously.

If you even agreed to this cruellest act, just despair. And if you need a rope, the thinnest thread a spider ever spun from her womb will be enough to strangle you; a reed will serve as a beam to hang you from. Or if you want to drown yourself, just put a little water in a spoon and it will be like the whole ocean, enough to choke such a villain. I suspect you very seriously.
If I in act, consent, or sin of thought, / Be guilty of the stealing that sweet breath / Which was embounded in this beauteous clay, / Let hell want pains enough to torture me! / I left him well.
If by act, consent, or the sin of a thought, I am guilty of stealing that sweet breath that was held in this beautiful body, let hell lack enough pains to torture me! I left him well.

Go, bear him in thine arms.— / I am amaz'd, methinks, and lose my way / Among the thorns and dangers of this world.— / How easy dost thou take all England up! / From forth this morsel of dead royalty, / The life, the right, and truth of all this realm / Is fled to heaven; and England now is left / To tug and scamble, and to part by the teeth / The unow'd interest of proud-swelling state. / Now for the bare-pick'd bone of majesty / Doth dogged war bristle his angry crest, / And snarleth in the gentle eyes of peace: / Now powers from home and discontents at home / Meet in one line; and vast confusion waits, / As doth a raven on a sick-fallen beast, / The imminent decay of wrested pomp. / Now happy he whose cloak and cincture can / Hold out this tempest.—Bear away that child, / And follow me with speed: I'll to the king; / A thousand businesses are brief in hand, / And heaven itself doth frown upon the land.

Go, carry him in your arms. I'm bewildered, I think, and losing my way among the thorns and dangers of this world. How easily you lift up all England! From this scrap of dead royalty, the life, the right and the truth of the whole realm have fled to heaven, and England is now left to fight and scramble and tear apart with its teeth the ownerless rights of a proud, swollen state. Now, over the bare-picked bone of kingship, snarling war raises its angry hackles and growls in the gentle face of peace. Now foreign armies and discontent at home line up together, and vast chaos waits, like a raven over a sick, fallen animal, for the coming collapse of seized power. Happy now is the man whose cloak and belt can hold out against this storm. Carry that child away and follow me quickly. I'm going to the King. A thousand urgent matters need doing, and heaven itself frowns on the land.
Thus have I yielded up into your hand / The circle of my glory.
So I have surrendered into your hand the circle of my glory.
Take again / From this my hand, as holding of the pope, / Your sovereign greatness and authority.
Take back from my hand, as held from the Pope, your sovereign greatness and authority.

Now keep your holy word: go meet the French; / And from his holiness use all your power / To stop their marches 'fore we are inflam'd. / Our discontented counties do revolt; / Our people quarrel with obedience; / Swearing allegiance and the love of soul / To stranger blood, to foreign royalty. / This inundation of mistemper'd humour / Rests by you only to be qualified. / Then pause not; for the present time's so sick / That present medicine must be ministr'd / Or overthrow incurable ensues.

Now keep your holy promise. Go and meet the French, and use all the power the Pope gives you to stop their advance before we are consumed by fire. Our discontented counties are in revolt. Our people dispute their duty of obedience, swearing loyalty and heartfelt love to foreign blood, foreign royalty. This flood of disordered feeling can only be calmed by you. So don't delay, because the times are so sick that medicine must be given now or an incurable collapse will follow.

It was my breath that blew this tempest up, / Upon your stubborn usage of the pope: / But since you are a gentle convertite, / My tongue shall hush again this storm of war / And make fair weather in your blustering land. / On this Ascension-day, remember well, / Upon your oath of service to the pope, / Go I to make the French lay down their arms.

It was my breath that blew up this storm, because of your stubborn treatment of the Pope. But since you are a gentle convert, my tongue will calm this storm of war again and make fair weather in your stormy land. Remember well: on this Ascension Day, because of your oath of service to the Pope, I am going to make the French lay down their arms.

Is this Ascension-day? Did not the prophet / Say that before Ascension-day at noon / My crown I should give off? Even so I have: / I did suppose it should be on constraint; / But, heaven be thank'd, it is but voluntary.
Is this Ascension Day? Didn't the prophet say that before noon on Ascension Day I'd give up my crown? And so I have. I thought it would be by force, but, thank heaven, it was voluntary.

All Kent hath yielded; nothing there holds out / But Dover Castle: London hath receiv'd, / Like a kind host, the Dauphin and his powers: / Your nobles will not hear you, but are gone / To offer service to your enemy; / And wild amazement hurries up and down / The little number of your doubtful friends.

All Kent has surrendered; nothing holds out there but Dover Castle. London has welcomed the Dauphin and his army like a kind host. Your nobles won't listen to you but have gone to offer their service to your enemy, and wild confusion rushes up and down among your few, doubtful friends.
Would not my lords return to me again / After they heard young Arthur was alive?
Didn't my lords come back to me when they heard young Arthur was alive?
They found him dead, and cast into the streets; / An empty casket, where the jewel of life / By some damn'd hand was robb'd and ta'en away.
They found him dead and thrown into the street, an empty casket from which some damned hand had stolen the jewel of life.
That villain Hubert told me he did live.
That villain Hubert told me he was alive.

So, on my soul, he did, for aught he knew. / But wherefore do you droop? why look you sad? / Be great in act, as you have been in thought; / Let not the world see fear and sad distrust / Govern the motion of a kingly eye: / Be stirring as the time; be fire with fire; / Threaten the threatener, and outface the brow / Of bragging horror: so shall inferior eyes, / That borrow their behaviours from the great, / Grow great by your example, and put on / The dauntless spirit of resolution. / Away, and glister like the god of war / When he intendeth to become the field: / Show boldness and aspiring confidence. / What, shall they seek the lion in his den, / And fright him there? and make him tremble there? / O, let it not be said!—Forage, and run / To meet displeasure farther from the doors, / And grapple with him ere he come so nigh.

And so, upon my soul, he was, as far as he knew. But why are you drooping? Why do you look sad? Be great in action, as you have been in thought. Don't let the world see fear and gloomy doubt govern the movement of a king's eye. Be as active as the times; meet fire with fire. Threaten the threatener and stare down the face of boasting terror. Then lesser eyes, which copy their behaviour from the great, will grow great by your example and take on the fearless spirit of resolve. Go, and shine like the god of war when he means to grace the battlefield. Show boldness and soaring confidence. What, will they seek the lion in his den and frighten him there, make him tremble there? Oh, don't let it be said! Go out and meet trouble further from your doors, and grapple with it before it comes so near.
The legate of the pope hath been with me, / And I have made a happy peace with him; / And he hath promis'd to dismiss the powers / Led by the Dauphin.
The Pope's legate has been with me, and I've made a happy peace with him. He has promised to send away the army led by the Dauphin.

O inglorious league! / Shall we, upon the footing of our land, / Send fair-play orders, and make compromise, / Insinuation, parley, and base truce, / To arms invasive? shall a beardless boy, / A cocker'd silken wanton, brave our fields, / And flesh his spirit in a warlike soil, / Mocking the air with colours idly spread, / And find no check? Let us, my liege, to arms; / Perchance the cardinal cannot make your peace; / Or, if he do, let it at least be said / They saw we had a purpose of defence.

Oh, shameful alliance! Shall we, standing on our own soil, send polite orders and offer compromise, flattery, talks and a base truce to invading armies? Shall a beardless boy, a pampered, silk-clad brat, defy us in our own fields, blood his spirit on warlike ground and mock the air with his banners lazily unfurled, and meet no resistance? Let us take up arms, my lord. Perhaps the cardinal can't make your peace, or if he does, at least let it be said they saw we meant to defend ourselves.
Have thou the ordering of this present time.
You take charge of matters now.
Away, then, with good courage! yet, I know / Our party may well meet a prouder foe.
Away, then, with good courage! And yet I know our side could well meet a prouder enemy.

My Lord Melun, let this be copied out / And keep it safe for our remembrance: / Return the precedent to these lords again; / That, having our fair order written down, / Both they and we, perusing o'er these notes, / May know wherefore we took the sacrament, / And keep our faiths firm and inviolable.

My Lord Melun, have this copied and keep it safe for our records. Give the original back to these lords, so that with our fair agreement written down, both they and we, reading these notes over, may know why we took the sacrament and keep our oaths firm and unbroken.

Upon our sides it never shall be broken. / And, noble Dauphin, albeit we swear / A voluntary zeal and an unurg'd faith / To your proceedings; yet, believe me, prince, / I am not glad that such a sore of time / Should seek a plaster by contemn'd revolt, / And heal the inveterate canker of one wound / By making many. O, it grieves my soul / That I must draw this metal from my side / To be a widow-maker! O, and there / Where honourable rescue and defence / Cries out upon the name of Salisbury! / But such is the infection of the time, / That, for the health and physic of our right, / We cannot deal but with the very hand / Of stern injustice and confused wrong.— / And is't not pity, O my grieved friends! / That we, the sons and children of this isle, / Were born to see so sad an hour as this; / Wherein we step after a stranger-march / Upon her gentle bosom, and fill up / Her enemies' ranks—I must withdraw and weep / Upon the spot of this enforc'd cause— / To grace the gentry of a land remote, / And follow unacquainted colours here? / What, here?—O nation, that thou couldst remove! / That Neptune's arms, who clippeth thee about, / Would bear thee from the knowledge of thyself, / And grapple thee unto a pagan shore, / Where these two Christian armies might combine / The blood of malice in a vein of league, / And not to spend it so unneighbourly!

On our side it will never be broken. And, noble Dauphin, though we swear willing zeal and unforced loyalty to your cause, believe me, prince, I am not glad that such a sore in our times has to look for a plaster in despised rebellion, and heal the deep-rooted ulcer of one wound by making many. Oh, it grieves my soul that I must draw this steel from my side to make widows, and in a place where honourable rescue and defence cry out against the name of Salisbury! But the times are so infected that, to heal and protect our rights, we can only act with the hand of harsh injustice and confused wrong. And isn't it a pity, oh my grieving friends, that we, the sons and children of this island, were born to see so sad an hour as this, when we march behind foreigners over her gentle breast and fill up her enemies' ranks (I must turn aside and weep at the shame of this forced cause), to honour the nobles of a distant land and follow strange flags here? What, here? Oh, my nation, if only you could move away! If only Neptune's arms, which hug you round, would carry you away from knowing yourself and fasten you to some pagan shore, where these two Christian armies could join their angry blood in one stream of alliance and not spill it so unneighbourly!

A noble temper dost thou show in this; / And great affections wrestling in thy bosom / Doth make an earthquake of nobility. / O, what a noble combat hast thou fought / Between compulsion and a brave respect! / Let me wipe off this honourable dew / That silverly doth progress on thy cheeks: / My heart hath melted at a lady's tears, / Being an ordinary inundation; / But this effusion of such manly drops, / This shower, blown up by tempest of the soul, / Startles mine eyes and makes me more amaz'd / Than had I seen the vaulty top of heaven / Figur'd quite o'er with burning meteors. / Lift up thy brow, renowned Salisbury, / And with a great heart heave away this storm: / Commend these waters to those baby eyes / That never saw the giant world enrag'd, / Nor met with fortune other than at feasts, / Full of warm blood, of mirth, of gossiping. / Come, come; for thou shalt thrust thy hand as deep / Into the purse of rich prosperity / As Louis himself:—so, nobles, shall you all, / That knit your sinews to the strength of mine.— / And even there, methinks, an angel spake: / Look, where the holy legate comes apace, / To give us warrant from the hand of heaven / And on our actions set the name of right / With holy breath.

You show a noble character in this, and the great feelings wrestling in your heart make an earthquake of nobility. Oh, what a noble fight you have fought between necessity and brave loyalty! Let me wipe away this honourable dew running silver down your cheeks. My heart has melted at a lady's tears, which are an ordinary flood, but this pouring of such manly drops, this shower blown up by a storm in the soul, startles my eyes and amazes me more than if I had seen the arched sky covered all over with blazing meteors. Lift up your face, famous Salisbury, and with a great heart throw off this storm. Leave these tears to those baby eyes that have never seen the giant world in a rage, or met Fortune anywhere but at feasts, full of warm blood, fun and chatter. Come, come, for you will thrust your hand as deep into the purse of rich success as Louis himself. So will all you nobles who bind your strength to mine. And just then, I think, an angel spoke. Look, here comes the holy legate in a hurry, to give us authority from the hand of heaven and set the name of right on our actions with his holy breath.

Hail, noble prince of France! / The next is this,—King John hath reconcil'd / Himself to Rome; his spirit is come in, / That so stood out against the holy church, / The great metropolis and see of Rome: / Therefore thy threatening colours now wind up, / And tame the savage spirit of wild war, / That, like a lion foster'd up at hand, / It may lie gently at the foot of peace / And be no further harmful than in show.

Greetings, noble Prince of France! The news is this: King John has reconciled himself with Rome. His spirit, which stood out so against the holy Church, the great capital and seat of Rome, has submitted. So now roll up your threatening banners and tame the savage spirit of wild war, so that, like a lion raised by hand, it may lie gently at the feet of peace and be harmful only in appearance.

Your grace shall pardon me, I will not back: / I am too high-born to be propertied, / To be a secondary at control, / Or useful serving-man and instrument / To any sovereign state throughout the world. / Your breath first kindled the dead coal of wars / Between this chastis'd kingdom and myself, / And brought in matter that should feed this fire; / And now 'tis far too huge to be blown out / With that same weak wind which enkindled it. / You taught me how to know the face of right, / Acquainted me with interest to this land, / Yea, thrust this enterprise into my heart; / And come ye now to tell me John hath made / His peace with Rome? What is that peace to me? / I, by the honour of my marriage-bed, / After young Arthur, claim this land for mine; / And, now it is half-conquer'd, must I back / Because that John hath made his peace with Rome? / Am I Rome's slave? What penny hath Rome borne, / What men provided, what munition sent, / To underprop this action? Is't not I / That undergo this charge? Who else but I, / And such as to my claim are liable, / Sweat in this business and maintain this war? / Have I not heard these islanders shout out, / 'Vive le roi!' as I have bank'd their towns? / Have I not here the best cards for the game, / To win this easy match, play'd for a crown? / And shall I now give o'er the yielded set? / No, no, on my soul, it never shall be said.

Your grace must pardon me. I won't go back. I'm too high-born to be used as property, to be someone's subordinate, or a useful servant and tool to any sovereign state in the world. Your breath first lit the dead coal of war between this punished kingdom and me, and brought fuel to feed the fire. Now it's far too big to be blown out by the same weak wind that lit it. You taught me to recognise my right, made me aware of my claim to this land, yes, pushed this enterprise into my heart. And now you come to tell me John has made his peace with Rome? What is that peace to me? By the honour of my marriage bed, I claim this land as mine after young Arthur. And now that it's half conquered, must I go back because John has made his peace with Rome? Am I Rome's slave? What penny has Rome paid, what men provided, what weapons sent, to support this campaign? Isn't it I who bear the cost? Who else but I and those bound to my claim sweat in this business and keep this war going? Haven't I heard these islanders shout "Long live the King!" as I passed their towns? Don't I hold the best cards to win this easy game, played for a crown? And shall I give up now, when the set is already won? No, no, on my soul, it will never be said.
You look but on the outside of this work.
You see only the outside of this business.

Outside or inside, I will not return / Till my attempt so much be glorified / As to my ample hope was promised / Before I drew this gallant head of war, / And cull'd these fiery spirits from the world, / To outlook conquest, and to win renown / Even in the jaws of danger and of death.—

Outside or inside, I won't go back until my enterprise has won as much glory as my great hopes were promised before I raised this splendid army and picked these fiery spirits from the world to stare down conquest and win fame even in the jaws of danger and death.
What lusty trumpet thus doth summon us?
What lively trumpet is calling us?

According to the fair play of the world, / Let me have audience; I am sent to speak:— / My holy lord of Milan, from the king / I come, to learn how you have dealt for him; / And, as you answer, I do know the scope / And warrant limited unto my tongue.

Following the fair customs of the world, let me be heard; I'm sent to speak. My holy lord of Milan, I come from the King to learn how you have done for him. Depending on your answer, I know the scope and authority given to my tongue.
The Dauphin is too wilful-opposite, / And will not temporize with my entreaties; / He flatly says he'll not lay down his arms.
The Dauphin is too wilfully opposed and won't bend to my pleas. He says flatly he won't lay down his arms.

By all the blood that ever fury breath'd, / The youth says well.—Now hear our English king; / For thus his royalty doth speak in me. / He is prepar'd; and reason too he should: / This apish and unmannerly approach, / This harness'd masque and unadvised revel / This unhair'd sauciness and boyish troops, / The king doth smile at; and is well prepar'd / To whip this dwarfish war, these pigmy arms, / From out the circle of his territories. / That hand which had the strength, even at your door, / To cudgel you, and make you take the hatch; / To dive, like buckets, in concealed wells; / To crouch in litter of your stable planks; / To lie, like pawns, lock'd up in chests and trunks; / To hug with swine; to seek sweet safety out / In vaults and prisons; and to thrill and shake / Even at the crying of your nation's crow, / Thinking this voice an armed Englishman;— / Shall that victorious hand be feebled here / That in your chambers gave you chastisement? / No: know the gallant monarch is in arms / And like an eagle o'er his aery towers / To souse annoyance that comes near his nest.— / And you degenerate, you ingrate revolts, / You bloody Neroes, ripping up the womb / Of your dear mother England, blush for shame; / For your own ladies and pale-visag'd maids, / Like Amazons, come tripping after drums,— / Their thimbles into armed gauntlets chang'd, / Their needles to lances, and their gentle hearts / To fierce and bloody inclination.

By all the blood that fury ever breathed, the youth speaks well! Now hear our English King, because his royalty speaks through me like this. He is prepared, and with good reason. This apish, ill-mannered approach, this masquerade in armour, this reckless party, this beardless cheek and these boyish troops, the King smiles at, and he is well prepared to whip this dwarfish war, these pygmy weapons, out of his territories. That hand which had the strength, even at your own doors, to beat you and make you jump over the half-door, to dive like buckets into hidden wells, to crouch in the straw of your stable floors, to lie locked up like pawned goods in chests and trunks, to hug pigs, to look for sweet safety in cellars and prisons, and to shudder and shake even at the crowing of your nation's cock, thinking its voice an armed Englishman: shall that victorious hand, which punished you in your own rooms, grow weak here? No. Know that the gallant King is armed, and like an eagle he soars over his nest to swoop on any threat that comes near it. And you degenerate, ungrateful rebels, you bloody Neros ripping open the womb of your dear mother England, blush for shame! Your own wives and pale-faced girls come tripping after drums like Amazons, their thimbles changed into armoured gloves, their needles into lances, and their gentle hearts into fierce and bloody impulses.
There end thy brave, and turn thy face in peace; / We grant thou canst outscold us: fare thee well; / We hold our time too precious to be spent / With such a brabbler.
End your bragging there and turn round in peace. We grant that you can out-scold us. Goodbye. Our time is too precious to waste on such a brawler.
We will attend to neither.— / Strike up the drums; and let the tongue of war, / Plead for our interest and our being here.
We'll listen to neither of you. Beat the drums, and let the tongue of war plead for our cause and our being here.

Indeed, your drums, being beaten, will cry out; / And so shall you, being beaten: do but start / And echo with the clamour of thy drum, / And even at hand a drum is ready brac'd / That shall reverberate all as loud as thine: / Sound but another, and another shall, / As loud as thine, rattle the welkin's ear, / And mock the deep-mouth'd thunder: for at hand,— / Not trusting to this halting legate here, / Whom he hath us'd rather for sport than need,— / Is warlike John; and in his forehead sits / A bare-ribb'd death, whose office is this day / To feast upon whole thousands of the French.

Indeed, your drums will cry out when beaten, and so will you when you're beaten. Just start one echoing with your drum's noise, and right at hand a drum is ready braced that will thunder back as loud as yours. Beat another, and another, as loud as yours, will rattle the sky's ear and mock the deep-voiced thunder. For near at hand, not relying on this limping legate here, whom he has used more for sport than need, is warlike John, and on his forehead sits bare-ribbed Death, whose job today is to feast on whole thousands of French.
Strike up our drums, to find this danger out.
Beat our drums, to find out this danger.
And thou shalt find it, Dauphin, do not doubt.
And you'll find it, Dauphin, don't doubt it.
How goes the day with us? O, tell me, Hubert.
How is the battle going for us? Oh, tell me, Hubert.
Badly, I fear. How fares your majesty?
Badly, I fear. How is your majesty?
This fever that hath troubled me so long / Lies heavy on me;—O, my heart is sick!
This fever that has troubled me so long lies heavy on me. Oh, my heart is sick!
My lord, your valiant kinsman, Falconbridge, / Desires your majesty to leave the field / And send him word by me which way you go.
My lord, your brave kinsman Falconbridge asks your majesty to leave the field and send word by me which way you are going.
Tell him, toward Swinstead, to the abbey there.
Tell him towards Swinstead, to the abbey there.

Be of good comfort; for the great supply / That was expected by the Dauphin here / Are wreck'd three nights ago on Goodwin Sands. / This news was brought to Richard but even now: / The French fight coldly, and retire themselves.

Take heart, because the great reinforcements the Dauphin was expecting here were wrecked three nights ago on the Goodwin Sands. This news reached Richard only just now. The French are fighting half-heartedly and pulling back.
Ay me! this tyrant fever burns me up / And will not let me welcome this good news.— / Set on toward Swinstead: to my litter straight; / Weakness possesseth me, and I am faint.
Oh no! This tyrant fever burns me up and won't let me welcome this good news. Go on towards Swinstead. To my litter at once. Weakness is taking hold of me, and I'm faint.
I did not think the king so stor'd with friends.
I didn't think the King had so many friends.
Up once again; put spirit in the French; / If they miscarry, we miscarry too.
Up once more; put some spirit into the French. If they fail, we fail too.
That misbegotten devil, Falconbridge, / In spite of spite, alone upholds the day.
That bastard devil Falconbridge, in spite of everything, is holding the day on his own.
They say King John, sore sick, hath left the field.
They say King John, very sick, has left the field.
Lead me to the revolts of England here.
Take me to the English rebels here.
When we were happy we had other names.
When we were happy we had other names.

Fly, noble English, you are bought and sold; / Unthread the rude eye of rebellion, / And welcome home again discarded faith. / Seek out King John, and fall before his feet; / For if the French be lords of this loud day, / He means to recompense the pains you take / By cutting off your heads: thus hath he sworn, / And I with him, and many more with me, / Upon the altar at Saint Edmunds-bury; / Even on that altar where we swore to you / Dear amity and everlasting love.

Run, noble English, you've been bought and sold! Pull your thread back out of the rough needle's eye of rebellion and welcome back the loyalty you threw away. Find King John and fall at his feet. Because if the French win this noisy day, he means to reward you for your trouble by cutting off your heads. He swore this, and I with him, and many more with me, on the altar at Saint Edmundsbury, the very altar where we swore dear friendship and everlasting love to you.
May this be possible? may this be true?
Can this be possible? Can this be true?

Have I not hideous death within my view, / Retaining but a quantity of life, / Which bleeds away even as a form of wax / Resolveth from his figure 'gainst the fire? / What in the world should make me now deceive, / Since I must lose the use of all deceit? / Why should I then be false, since it is true / That I must die here, and live hence by truth? / I say again, if Louis do win the day, / He is forsworn if e'er those eyes of yours / Behold another day break in the east: / But even this night,—whose black contagious breath / Already smokes about the burning crest / Of the old, feeble, and day-wearied sun,— / Even this ill night, your breathing shall expire; / Paying the fine of rated treachery / Even with a treacherous fine of all your lives, / If Louis by your assistance win the day. / Commend me to one Hubert, with your king; / The love of him,—and this respect besides, / For that my grandsire was an Englishman,— / Awakes my conscience to confess all this. / In lieu whereof, I pray you, bear me hence / From forth the noise and rumour of the field, / Where I may think the remnant of my thoughts / In peace, and part this body and my soul / With contemplation and devout desires.

Don't I have hideous death in front of my eyes, with only a little life left, which bleeds away just as a wax figure melts out of shape in front of the fire? What in the world could make me deceive now, when I'm about to lose all use for deceit? Why should I be false, when it's true that I must die here and live hereafter only through truth? I say again: if Louis wins the day, he will be breaking his oath if your eyes ever see another day dawn in the east. This very night, whose black, infectious breath already smokes around the burning crown of the old, feeble, day-weary sun, this very evil night, you will breathe your last, paying the penalty for your treachery with the treacherous loss of all your lives, if Louis wins the day with your help. Give my regards to a man called Hubert, who is with your King. My love for him, and the fact that my grandfather was an Englishman, wakes my conscience to confess all this. In return, I beg you, carry me away from the noise and din of the battlefield, where I can think my last thoughts in peace and part my body and soul with meditation and devout prayers.

We do believe thee:—and beshrew my soul / But I do love the favour and the form / Of this most fair occasion, by the which / We will untread the steps of damned flight; / And like a bated and retired flood, / Leaving our rankness and irregular course, / Stoop low within those bounds we have o'erlook'd, / And calmly run on in obedience / Even to our ocean, to our great King John.— / My arm shall give thee help to bear thee hence; / For I do see the cruel pangs of death / Right in thine eye.—Away, my friends! New flight, / And happy newness, that intends old right.

We believe you. And curse my soul if I don't love the look and shape of this fair chance, by which we will retrace the steps of our damned desertion, and, like a flood that has gone down and drawn back, leaving our swollen, wandering course, sink low within the banks we overflowed and run calmly in obedience to our ocean, our great King John. My arm will help carry you away, because I can see the cruel pangs of death right in your eye. Away, my friends! A new flight, and a happy change that aims at old loyalty.

The sun of heaven, methought, was loath to set, / But stay'd, and made the western welkin blush, / When the English measur'd backward their own ground / In faint retire. O, bravely came we off, / When with a volley of our needless shot, / After such bloody toil, we bid good night; / And wound our tattering colours clearly up, / Last in the field, and almost lords of it!

The sun in the sky, I thought, was reluctant to set, and stayed and made the western sky blush, when the English retreated weakly over their own ground. Oh, we came off bravely, when, after such bloody work, we said goodnight with a volley of unnecessary shots and rolled up our tattered flags, last on the field and almost its masters!
Where is my prince, the Dauphin?
Where is my prince, the Dauphin?
The Count Melun is slain; the English lords / By his persuasion are again fall'n off: / And your supply, which you have wish'd so long, / Are cast away and sunk on Goodwin Sands.
Count Melun is killed. The English lords, persuaded by him, have deserted again. And your reinforcements, which you've wanted for so long, are wrecked and sunk on the Goodwin Sands.

Ah, foul shrewd news!—beshrew thy very heart!— / I did not think to be so sad to-night / As this hath made me.—Who was he that said / King John did fly an hour or two before / The stumbling night did part our weary powers?

Ah, foul, cruel news! Curse your very heart! I didn't expect to be as sad tonight as this has made me. Who was it who said King John fled an hour or two before stumbling night separated our weary armies?
Whoever spoke it, it is true, my lord.
Whoever said it, it's true, my lord.
Keep good quarter and good care to-night; / The day shall not be up so soon as I, / To try the fair adventure of to-morrow.
Keep good watch and take good care tonight. The day won't be up as early as I will, to try our fortune tomorrow.
Who's there? speak, ho! speak quickly, or I shoot.
Who's there? Speak, ho! Speak quickly, or I'll shoot.
What's that to thee? Why may I not demand / Of thine affairs, as well as thou of mine?
What's that to you? Why can't I ask about your business as well as you about mine?
Thou hast a perfect thought: / I will, upon all hazards, well believe / Thou art my friend that know'st my tongue so well. / Who art thou?
You think rightly. Whatever the risk, I'll believe you're my friend, since you know my voice so well. Who are you?
Who thou wilt: and if thou please, / Thou mayst befriend me so much as to think / I come one way of the Plantagenets.
Whoever you like. And if you please, you can be friendly enough to think I'm descended on one side from the Plantagenets.
Unkind remembrance! thou and eyeless night / Have done me shame:—brave soldier, pardon me, / That any accent breaking from thy tongue / Should scape the true acquaintance of mine ear.
Cruel memory! You and blind night have shamed me. Brave soldier, forgive me that any sound from your tongue should escape my ear's true recognition.
Come, come; sans compliment, what news abroad?
Come, come, no ceremony. What news?
Why, here walk I, in the black brow of night, / To find you out.
Why, here I am, walking in the black face of night to find you.
Brief, then; and what's the news?
O, my sweet sir, news fitting to the night, / Black, fearful, comfortless, and horrible.
Oh, my dear sir, news to suit the night: black, fearful, comfortless and horrible.
Show me the very wound of this ill news; / I am no woman, I'll not swoon at it.
Show me the very wound of this bad news. I'm no woman; I won't faint at it.

The king, I fear, is poison'd by a monk: / I left him almost speechless and broke out / To acquaint you with this evil, that you might / The better arm you to the sudden time, / Than if you had at leisure known of this.

The King, I fear, has been poisoned by a monk. I left him almost speechless and rushed out to tell you of this evil, so that you could prepare yourself better for the emergency than if you'd heard of it at leisure.
How did he take it; who did taste to him?
How did he take it? Who tasted his food for him?
A monk, I tell you; a resolved villain, / Whose bowels suddenly burst out: the king / Yet speaks, and peradventure may recover.
A monk, I tell you, a determined villain, whose insides suddenly burst. The King still speaks and may perhaps recover.
Who didst thou leave to tend his majesty?
Whom did you leave to look after his majesty?
Why, know you not? The lords are all come back, / And brought Prince Henry in their company; / At whose request the king hath pardon'd them, / And they are all about his majesty.
Why, don't you know? The lords have all come back and brought Prince Henry with them. At his request the King has pardoned them, and they are all around his majesty.

Withhold thine indignation, mighty heaven, / And tempt us not to bear above our power!— / I'll tell thee, Hubert, half my power this night, / Passing these flats, are taken by the tide,— / These Lincoln washes have devoured them; / Myself, well-mounted, hardly have escap'd. / Away, before! conduct me to the king; / I doubt he will be dead or ere I come.

Hold back your anger, mighty heaven, and don't test us beyond what we can bear! I'll tell you, Hubert: half my army, crossing these flats tonight, were caught by the tide. These Lincolnshire Wash marshes swallowed them. I barely escaped myself, and I was well mounted. Go on ahead! Take me to the King. I'm afraid he'll be dead before I get there.

It is too late: the life of all his blood / Is touch'd corruptibly, and his pure brain,— / Which some suppose the soul's frail dwelling-house,— / Doth, by the idle comments that it makes, / Foretell the ending of mortality.
It's too late. All his blood's life is fatally infected, and his pure brain, which some think is the soul's fragile house, foretells the end of his life through the wandering things it says.
His Highness yet doth speak; and holds belief / That, being brought into the open air, / It would allay the burning quality / Of that fell poison which assaileth him.
His highness is still speaking, and believes that if he is brought into the open air it would cool the burning of the deadly poison attacking him.
Let him be brought into the orchard here.— / Doth he still rage?
Have him brought into the orchard here. Is he still raving?
He is more patient / Than when you left him; even now he sung.
He is calmer than when you left him. Just now he was singing.

O vanity of sickness! fierce extremes / In their continuance will not feel themselves. / Death, having prey'd upon the outward parts, / Leaves them invisible; and his siege is now / Against the mind, the which he pricks and wounds / With many legions of strange fantasies, / Which, in their throng and press to that last hold, / Confound themselves. 'Tis strange that death should sing.— / I am the cygnet to this pale faint swan, / Who chants a doleful hymn to his own death; / And from the organ-pipe of frailty sings / His soul and body to their lasting rest.

Oh, the delusions of sickness! Fierce extremes, if they go on, stop feeling themselves. Death, having fed on the outer body, leaves it numb, and now he is besieging the mind, pricking and wounding it with legions of strange fantasies, which, crowding and pushing towards that last stronghold, destroy themselves. It's strange that death should sing. I am the young swan to this pale, faint swan, who sings a mournful hymn at his own death, and from the frail organ-pipe of his throat sings his soul and body to their eternal rest.
Be of good comfort, prince; for you are born / To set a form upon that indigest / Which he hath left so shapeless and so rude.
Take heart, prince, for you were born to give shape to the chaos he has left so shapeless and rough.

Ay, marry, now my soul hath elbow-room; / It would not out at windows nor at doors. / There is so hot a summer in my bosom / That all my bowels crumble up to dust; / I am a scribbled form, drawn with a pen, / Upon a parchment; and against this fire / Do I shrink up.

Yes, now my soul has room to move. It wouldn't go out by the windows or the doors. There is so hot a summer in my chest that all my insides crumble into dust. I am a scribbled figure, drawn with a pen on parchment, and I shrivel up against this fire.

Poison'd,—ill-fare;—dead, forsook, cast off; / And none of you will bid the winter come, / To thrust his icy fingers in my maw; / Nor let my kingdom's rivers take their course / Through my burn'd bosom; nor entreat the north / To make his bleak winds kiss my parched lips, / And comfort me with cold:—I do not ask you much; / I beg cold comfort; and you are so strait, / And so ingrateful, you deny me that.

Poisoned, badly; dead, abandoned, thrown away. And none of you will tell winter to come and thrust its icy fingers into my stomach, or let my kingdom's rivers run through my burnt chest, or beg the north to make its bleak winds kiss my parched lips and comfort me with cold. I'm not asking much: I beg for cold comfort, and you are so stingy and ungrateful that you deny me even that.
O, that there were some virtue in my tears, / That might relieve you!
Oh, if only my tears had some power to relieve you!
The salt in them is hot.— / Within me is a hell; and there the poison / Is, as a fiend, confin'd to tyrannize / On unreprievable condemned blood.
The salt in them is hot. There is a hell inside me, and the poison is shut up there like a fiend, tormenting my blood, which is condemned beyond reprieve.
O, I am scalded with my violent motion / And spleen of speed to see your majesty!
Oh, I'm scalded from my rushing and the fury of my speed to see your majesty!

O cousin, thou art come to set mine eye: / The tackle of my heart is crack'd and burn'd; / And all the shrouds, wherewith my life should sail, / Are turned to one thread, one little hair: / My heart hath one poor string to stay it by, / Which holds but till thy news be uttered; / And then all this thou seest is but a clod, / And module of confounded royalty.

Oh, cousin, you've come to close my eyes. The rigging of my heart is cracked and burnt, and all the ropes my life should sail by have turned to a single thread, one little hair. My heart has one poor string to hold it, which will last only until your news is spoken, and then all you see here is just a lump of earth, the mere shape of ruined royalty.

The Dauphin is preparing hitherward, / Where heaven he knows how we shall answer him; / For in a night the best part of my power, / As I upon advantage did remove, / Were in the washes all unwarily / Devoured by the unexpected flood.

The Dauphin is preparing to come this way, and heaven knows how we'll answer him, because in one night the best part of my army, as I moved them for a better position, was carelessly swallowed by the unexpected flood in the Wash.
You breathe these dead news in as dead an ear. / My liege! my lord!—But now a king,—now thus.
You're speaking dead news into an ear just as dead. My liege! My lord! A king just now, and now like this.
Even so must I run on, and even so stop. / What surety of the world, what hope, what stay, / When this was now a king, and now is clay?
I too must run my course and stop just like this. What certainty is there in the world, what hope, what support, when this was a king a moment ago and now is clay?

Art thou gone so? I do but stay behind / To do the office for thee of revenge, / And then my soul shall wait on thee to heaven, / As it on earth hath been thy servant still.— / Now, now, you stars that move in your right spheres, / Where be your powers? Show now your mended faiths; / And instantly return with me again, / To push destruction and perpetual shame / Out of the weak door of our fainting land. / Straight let us seek, or straight we shall be sought; / The Dauphin rages at our very heels.

Have you gone like this? I'm only staying behind to take revenge for you, and then my soul will follow you to heaven as it has always served you on earth. Now, now, you stars, back in your proper orbits, where are your forces? Show your restored loyalty now, and come back with me at once to drive destruction and lasting shame out through the weak door of our fainting land. Let's seek the enemy at once, or at once he'll seek us. The Dauphin is raging at our heels.

It seems you know not, then, so much as we: / The Cardinal Pandulph is within at rest, / Who half an hour since came from the Dauphin, / And brings from him such offers of our peace / As we with honour and respect may take, / With purpose presently to leave this war.

It seems you don't know as much as we do, then. Cardinal Pandulph is resting inside. He came from the Dauphin half an hour ago and brings offers of peace from him that we can accept with honour and respect, intending to give up this war at once.
He will the rather do it when he sees / Ourselves well sinewed to our defence.
He'll be all the readier to do it when he sees us strongly prepared to defend ourselves.

Nay, 'tis in a manner done already; / For many carriages he hath despatch'd / To the sea-side, and put his cause and quarrel / To the disposing of the cardinal: / With whom yourself, myself, and other lords, / If you think meet, this afternoon will post / To consummate this business happily.

No, it's more or less done already. He has sent many wagons of baggage to the coast and left his cause and quarrel in the cardinal's hands. With him you, I and other lords, if you think fit, will hurry this afternoon to bring this business to a happy end.
Let it be so:—And you, my noble prince, / With other princes that may best be spar'd, / Shall wait upon your father's funeral.
So be it. And you, my noble prince, with the other nobles who can best be spared, will attend your father's funeral.
At Worcester must his body be interr'd; / For so he will'd it.
His body must be buried at Worcester, because he wished it so.

Thither shall it, then: / And happily may your sweet self put on / The lineal state and glory of the land! / To whom, with all submission, on my knee, / I do bequeath my faithful services / And true subjection everlastingly.
Then it will go there. And may your sweet self happily take on the inherited rank and glory of the land! To you, on my knee, with all submission, I give my faithful service and true loyalty for ever.
And the like tender of our love we make, / To rest without a spot for evermore.
And we make the same offer of our love, to remain without a stain for ever.
I have a kind soul that would give you thanks, / And knows not how to do it but with tears.
I have a kind soul that would like to thank you and doesn't know how to do it except with tears.

O, let us pay the time but needful woe, / Since it hath been beforehand with our griefs.— / This England never did, nor never shall, / Lie at the proud foot of a conqueror, / But when it first did help to wound itself. / Now these her princes are come home again, / Come the three corners of the world in arms, / And we shall shock them: nought shall make us rue, / If England to itself do rest but true.

Oh, let us give the times only the grief they need, since they have already paid our sorrows in advance. This England never did and never will lie at the proud foot of a conqueror, except when it first helped to wound itself. Now that her nobles have come home again, let the three corners of the world come against us in arms, and we will shock them. Nothing will make us regret, if England only stays true to itself.
